(Admin); Comparable Properties; Appeal Dismissed

DECISION AND STATEMENT OF REASONS

DECISION 
 
1. 
The appeal is dismissed. 
 
2. 
The valuation Band was confirmed in Band B with effect from 1 April 1993. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
This appeal has been brought in respect of 171 Church Street, Ripley DE5 9TE. A proposal 
was served on the Listing Officer by the appellant, in dispute of the Band B assessment and 
seeking a reduction to Band A. The Listing Officer reviewed the Band and, on 14 January 
2026, issued a decision notice confirming the property in Band B with effect from 1 April 
1993. 
 
4. 
In this appeal, the relevant date for consideration of the physical state of the dwelling and its 
locality was 1 April 1993, the date the subject property entered the valuation list 
 
5. 
Prior to this hearing the appellant had requested that this matter be heard in her absence 
based on the evidence provided. 
 
6. 
This statement of reasons is not and does not purport to be a full verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Background 
 
7. 
On her appeal form the appellant stated as follows: 
 
“The listing officer compared my property 171 Church street with 102 and 100a Church 
street, these are not comparable properties 102 and 100a are much newer properties with 
Garages and may not have existed in 1993. My property is no different to 167 Church Street, 
which adjoins the same block of as 171 with 169 in between. 167 and 171 are identical 
properties, both having later building additions. 171 has a slightly larger entrance to the side 
of the property that 167 but they have very similar size plots of land, 167 also has a parking 
space to the front of the property, I do not agree that 171 is a band B if 167 is a band A. they 
are basically the same 2 up 2 down property built at the same time.  
Therefore 171 is not comparable with 100a but is comparable with 167 so I would appreciate 
this being reassessed and do not accept the listing officer’s decision.” 
 
8. 
The subject property is an end terraced house built pre-1919. Within the 93m2 reduced 
covered area (RCA), there are three bedrooms, two bathrooms, one reception room and a 
kitchen. The property also benefits from a conservatory and off street parking. 
 
9. 
For council tax purposes, domestic dwellings are measured to RCA. In brief, this is the area 
of a building measured externally at each floor level and includes perimeter wall thickness, 
external projections (such as a bay), and areas occupied by internal walls, partitions and 
stairwells. Measurements are done in this way to give uniformity and fairness and facilitates 
easy comparison between dwellings. Loft conversions with sloping ceilings are calculated on 
external areas any internal areas with a head height of below 1.5m2 are excluded. 
Additionally, garages are excluded from the RCA. 
 

[2026] VTE VT00034997 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
3/5 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
Relevant Law 
 
10. The panel had regard to the legislation for council tax and, in particular, the Council Tax 
(Situation and Valuation of Dwellings) Regulations 1992, which amongst other things, 
required that the value of a domestic property for council tax Banding purposes was the 
amount which it might reasonably have been expected to realise had it been sold on the 
open market by a willing vendor on the antecedent valuation day (AVD) 1 April 1991. 
 
11. Under regulation 6 of the Council Tax (Situation and Valuation of Dwellings) Regulations 
1992 (SI 1992 No. 550), each valuation Band represents a value that a dwelling might 
reasonably have been expected to realise. The Bands are set out in section 5(2) of the Local 
Government Finance Act 1992, with the relevant Bands in relation to this appeal being:   
 
Band A – values not exceeding £40,000; and 
Band B – values exceeding £40,000 but not exceeding £52,000. 
 
Discussion 
 
12. Therefore, regardless of whether a property existed on 1 April 1991, or was purchased at a 
later date, in order to allow fairness and uniformity between all council tax valuations, all 
domestic property must be valued at the common date of 1 April 1991 and the level of value 
on that date, albeit within a range of values, had to be determined. 
 
13. Band A represents properties with a range of values not exceeding £40,000 as at 1 April 
1991; therefore, for the appeal to be successful and the Band to be reduced it must be 
shown that the subject property would have sold for less than £40,000 on 1 April 1991 
 
14. The best evidence on which to determine the Band of a property was therefore considered to 
be an open market sale of either the subject property, or of ones which are comparable with 
it, that had completed on or close to the valuation date of 1 April 1991. 
 
15. The Listing Officer had provided sales evidence for four properties which, Mrs Fisher 
submitted, were comparable and supported Band B for the subject property. In particular the 
panel noted that: 152, Nottingham Road, Ripley, was a two bedroom, one bathroom end-
terraced house with an RCA of 65m2, it had sold for £38,500 on 15 May 1991; 60, Pease Hill 
Road, Ripley, was a two bedroom, one bathroom end-terraced house with an RCA of 61m2, it 
had sold for £39,950 on 26 April 1991; and 103, Pentrich Road, Ripley, was a two bedroom 
one bathroom end-terraced house with an RCA of 73m2 it had sold for £37,500 on 26 April 
1991. The panel found this evidence to be of some significance, it noted that these properties 
were of notably smaller than the subject property and had sold very close to the AVD, it 
determined that these sales supported Band B for the subject property which was in the 
same location and had an RCA of 93m2 which included a third bedroom and a second 
bathroom.  
 
16. The panel determined that had the subject property been placed for sale on the open market 
on 1 April 1991 it would probably have achieved a sales value above the lower band B 
threshold. 
 
17. The panel was aware that a property’s Banding could be determined by tone, should the 
‘tone of the list’ have been established. A tone of value/Band is established when a number 
of properties, similar in size, character, quality, detachment and location were attributed the 
same level of assessment/Band which, over time, had not been challenged. Assessments 

[2026] VTE VT00034997 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
4/5 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
that had been challenged and subsequently agreed by parties or determined by a Tribunal 
panel were also instrumental in establishing the tone. Mrs Fisher referred to 12, Pit Lane, 
Waingroves, Ripley, and 61, Queen Street, Waingroves, Ripley, which were also three-
bedroom terraced houses with two bathrooms, they RCA’s of 108m2 and 102m2 respectively 
and were all in Band B. 
 
18. The panel noted that these properties were larger than the subject property and that 12, Pit 
Lane, had a garage, however, it was aware that band B comprised a wide bandwidth, which 
included properties with capital values as at 1 April 1991 levels exceeding £40,000 but not 
exceeding £52,000. As such, the panel held that band B was large enough to encompass a 
range of property types and sizes. Furthermore, the panel identified that the subject property 
had been ascribed Band B since the valuation list was compiled and there appeared to be a 
settled tone of Banding in the road. As the valuation list had been in force for over 30 years, 
the panel found that the tone should only be disturbed when there is strong evidence to do 
so. 
 
19. The panel turned to the evidence submitted by the appellant including 167, 169 and 173 
Church Street in Waingroves. The panel noted that these properties were smaller than the 
subject property when they were ascribed band A. The appellant had also referred to four 
properties which appeared to be larger than the subject property and in band A. The panel 
was aware that three of the four properties were marked to be reviewed it was aware that the 
banding of similar properties can appear inconsistent for the following reasons:  
 
• Properties which had been extended but not yet sold. The Listing Officer is 
unable to review the Band of an extended/improved property until there has 
been a relevant transaction, e.g., a sale. 
• Properties that had been extended and subsequently sold but not yet 
reviewed. The Listing Officer relies upon reports from the Billing Authority to 
notify any changes to a property 
 
20. The appellant had referred to the Nationwide House Price Index and sales of the subject 
property in 2014 and 2025. The panel viewed the calculations with caution as it was aware 
that house price calculators and indices were by their very nature unreliable for council tax 
purposes and, therefore, of little assistance, as they covered a wide geographic area, which 
contained great variation between different localities and included different types of 
properties. For the purposes of this particular appeal, the panel was solely concerned with 
terraced houses in the immediate vicinity and sales close to the AVD, house price 
calculators/indices did not provide the level of detail required. The panel, therefore, attached 
little weight to this evidence.  
 
21. The appellant had also referred to four Energy Performance Certificates to demonstrate the 
size of various properties, unfortunately the panel was aware that these certificates do not 
reflect the method of measuring used for council tax which is out lined in paragraph nine 
above. 
 
22. In appeals of this nature, the legal burden of proof rests upon the appellant to show that the 
current Band is incorrect. Considering the evidence before it, the panel held that insufficient 
evidence had been provided to demonstrate that the Band B assessment was excessive. 
 
Conclusion

23. In view of the above findings and conclusions, the appeal was dismissed. 
 
Right of further appeal 
 
24. Any party who is aggrieved at the Tribunal’s decision has a statutory right of further appeal to 
the High Court on a point of law pursuant to Regulation 43 of the Tribunal Procedure 
Regulations. A party does not require permission to appeal from the Tribunal. Any appeal 
must be made directly to the High Court using Form N161 (Appellant’s Notice) within four 
weeks of the date this decision and statement of reasons was issued. 
 
25. Further information regarding this statutory right of further appeal, and the parties’ other 
rights, is contained in the guidance booklet “A guide to tribunal decisions” available on the 
Tribunal’s website at www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk/guidance-booklets/.

of the Local Government Finance Act 1992; Wilson v Josephine Coll (Listing Officer) [2011] EWHC 
2824 (Admin); Bunyan v Patel [2022] EWHC 1143 (Admin); hereditament test; property capable of
repair; section 66(5) of the Local Government Finance Act 1988; vacant property; appeal dismissed
 
Before:

DECISION AND STATEMENT OF REASONS

DECISION 
 
1. 
The appeal is dismissed. 
 
2. 
The panel upheld the Listing Officer’s decision not to delete the subject property’s entry from 
the Valuation List. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
The appeal began with a proposal made on 13 June 2025, which sought the deletion of Flat 
18A, Charteris Road, London NW67ET, from the Valuation List. On 30 October 2025 the 
Listing Officer issued a decision notice making no alteration to the Valuation List. The 
appellant made an appeal to this Tribunal on 17 January 2025 in respect of that decision, as 
he believed the subject property should be deleted from the list because it was unhabitable. 
 
4. 
The “relevant date” for the purposes of this appeal was 31 March 2025, this being the date 
the appellant proposed the entry should be deleted. 
 
5. 
With the agreement of the parties and to assist the appellant, the panel varied Practice 
Statement 8 (the Model Hearing Procedure) and invited the respondent's representative to 
present his evidence first. 
 
6. 
The Tribunal panel conducted the hearing of this appeal remotely via Microsoft Teams 
conference call using audio/video-link. Prior to the hearing, the appellant advised the Tribunal 
that due to a poor connection he would be unable to make a video connection to the hearing 
room. However, that was resolved, and the clerk called the appellant into the hearing by 
audio link. For the avoidance of any doubt, the panel was satisfied that those present at the 
hearing were able to fully participate in the proceedings. 
 
7. 
This statement of reasons is not and does not purport to be a full verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Background 
 
8. 
On his appeal for the appellant stated as follows: 
 
“Contrary to the assertion of the VOA case worker, the property is not "watertight", as 
(evidenced by Jason Ginn's Trace and Access Report), it is infested with pervasive rising 
damp, which has used itself as a vessel to travel the whole property. This is as a result of a 
botched conversion, including communal pipes not affixed to drainage, resulting in long term 
water ingress (the magnitude picked up neither by survey nor damp report). VOA state, "if 
you are living in property, or it is capable of being lived in, we will not delete" - I am not, 
precisely because flat is not capable of being lived in from the point of view of health -I have 
asthma; have submitted photographs evidencing damp, a bedroom which is a dust infested 
building site, a bathroom minus sink. The VOA website states stripping out of floors 
considered major renovation -Jason Ginn's schedule of works advocates exactly that, as 
damp now lurks behind every surface. The VOA's website also states although mould does 
not constitute sufficient reason for deletion, rising damp does (which is why the government 
now, perpetually, warns of its dangers -everything wrong with Charteris is damp related” 
 

[2026] VTE VT00035003 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
3/6 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
9. 
The Listing Officer did not consider that the property was beyond reasonable repair on the 
relevant date and therefore argued that the property should remain in the list. The following 
case law had been referred to: 
 
• Wilson v Coll (LO) [2011] EWHC 2824 (Admin) 
• Bunyan (LO) v Patel [2022] EWHC 1143 (Admin) 
• SJ & J Monk (A Firm) v Newbigin (Valuation Officer) [2017] UKSC 14 
• Jackson (VO) v Canary Wharf Limited [2019] UKUT 136 (LC) 
 
10.  
 
Relevant Law 
 
11. The panel turned to the relevant legislation and case law. 
 
12. The legal basis of a dwelling for council tax purposes is that it must constitute a 
hereditament, in accordance with section 3 of the Local Government Finance Act 1992:   
 
(i) 
Meaning of “dwelling” 
(ii) 
3(1) This section has effect for determining what is a dwelling for the 
purposes of this Part. 
(iii) 3(2) Subject to the following provisions of this section, a dwelling is any 
property which – by virtue of the definition of hereditament in section 115(1) 
of the General Rate Act 1967, would have been a hereditament for the 
purposes of that Act if that Act remained in force; and is not for the time being 
shown or required to be shown in a local or a central non-domestic rating list 
in force at that time; 
 
13. Section 115(1) of the General Rate Act 1967 defined a hereditament as: 
 
1. In this Act, except where the context otherwise requires, the following expressions have 
the following meanings respectively, that is to say – 
 
“hereditament” means property, which is or may become liable to a rate, being a unit 
of such property, which is, or would fall to be, shown as a separate item in the 
Valuation List. 
 
14. The Council Tax (Situation and Valuation of Dwellings) Regulations 1992 Statutory 
Instrument No. 550. 
 
Valuation of dwellings: general 
 
6. (1) Subject to regulation 7. For the purposes of valuations under Section 21 (valuations for  
purposes of lists) of the Act, the value of any dwelling shall be taken to be the amount which  
on certain assumptions (mentioned in paragraph (2) and (3) below), the dwelling might  
reasonably have been expected to realise if it had been sold in the open market by a willing  
vendor on 1 April 1991.  
 
(2) The assumptions are: 
 
(a) that the sale was with vacant possession 

[2026] VTE VT00035003 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
4/6 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
(b) that the interest sold was the freehold or in the case of a flat, a lease for 99 years 
at a nominal rent 
(c) that the dwelling was sold free from any rent charge or other incumbrance 
(d) except in a case to which paragraph (3) applies that the size, layout and 
character of the dwelling and the physical state of its locality were the same as at the 
relevant date 
(e) that the dwelling was in a state of reasonable repair …… 
 
15. Thus, under the statutory scheme, in appeals of this nature, a determination of whether a 
hereditament existed was required. The essential elements of rateable occupation which 
have to be met in order for a hereditament to exist have been considered by the courts in a 
number of different statutory contexts. 
 
16. In John Laing & Son Limited v Assessment Committee for Kingswood Assessment Area & 
Others [1949] 1 KB 344, Tucker LJ said at 350: 
 
 “Mr. Rowe has said that there are four necessary ingredients in rateable 
occupation, and I do not think there is any controversy with regard to those 
ingredients. First, there must be actual occupation; secondly, that it must be 
exclusive for the particular purposes of the possessor; thirdly, that the possession 
must be of some value or benefit to the possessor; and, fourthly, the possession 
must not be for too transient a period….” 
 
17. As to whether a dwelling exists, the law as expounded in the High Court judgment of Wilson 
v Coll was relevant in this case. The hereditament test was approved by Mr Justice Singh, 
and in paragraph 39 and 40 he confirmed: 
 
“39. In answering that question correctly, the Respondent submitted to me that what 
in fact should be asked is a question which is posed for Listing Officers to consider in 
Practice Note 4: Disrepair, Building Works, Temporary Disabilities and Flooding to 
the Council Tax Manual (Valuation Office Agency). The question is: “Having regard to 
the character of the property and a reasonable amount of repair works being 
undertaken could the premises be occupied as a dwelling? 
 
40. I accept that as a general matter of law the crucial distinction for the purposes of 
deciding whether there is, or continues to be, a hereditament should focus upon 
whether a property is capable of being rendered suitable for occupation (in the 
present context occupation as a dwelling) by undertaking a reasonable amount of 
repair works. The distinction, which is correctly drawn by the respondent, in my view, 
is between a truly derelict property, which is incapable of being repaired to make it 
suitable for its intended purpose, and repair which would render it capable again of 
being occupied for the purposes for which it is intended.” 
 
18. In Bunyan v Patel, Mrs Justice Lang affirmed the hereditament test expounded in Wilson v 
Coll as the correct test to be applied when determining whether a hereditament was still in 
existence. It was held that the test was also consistent with the judgment of the Supreme 
Court in Newbigin v Monk. In Mrs Justice Lang’s judgment, she endorsed sections of the 
VOA’s Council Tax Manual Practice Note No 4 regarding deletions from the Valuation List 
which also gave reference to the Newbigin v Monk judgment. 
 
Discussion 
 

[2026] VTE VT00035003 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
5/6 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
19. The panel paid particular attention to the Supreme Court judgement in Newbigin v Monk 
[2017]. That was a non-domestic rating case which concerned an office building in the 
process of being redeveloped. The outcome of the case was that once a schedule of works 
had been produced, and work had started to redevelop the space, the office was no longer 
capable of beneficial occupation and therefore was not a hereditament and should be 
removed from the rating list. In the case before it, the panel had been presented with no 
evidence to suggest that there was a schedule of works for the subject property. 
 
20. At the hearing the appellant reiterated the arguments made on his appeal form, he stated 
that the subject property had a major problem with rising damp, water ingress and mould and 
he had provided reports, photographs and quotes to evidence this. He also stated that the 
property could not be occupied due to noxious gases but there was nothing provided in 
evidence to support this statement. The panel noted that the report on the property had been 
made in July 2025, several months after the relevant date and that the property was now 
habitable. It was also noted that on questioning the appellant stated that up to the relevant 
date, which was the date of purchase, the property was being inhabited ‘on and off’ as it was 
being let as an Airbnb. 
 
21. Following the High Court judgment Bunyan v Patel, the panel considered that there was a 
very high bar to overcome before a property could be deleted from the Valuation List. In the 
case before it, it would have to be shown that as at the relevant date, the subject property 
was incapable of being reasonably repaired and therefore failed to constitute a hereditament 
in line with the test in Wilson v Coll. 
 
22. Whilst the panel noted the situation the appellant found himself in, it was aware that it is 
bound by judgments of higher courts and that in Wilson v Coll, Mr Justice Singh held that the 
question did not turn on whether it would be financially viable to carry out the repairs but 
whether the property is reasonably capable of repair without changing its essential character. 
It found that this was an important factor in the Wilson v Coll decision as it meant that the test 
was simply one of whether the dwelling was capable of repair, rather than whether it would 
be repaired. 
 
23. Mr Dakin had contended that the condition of the property at the relevant date was not 
shown to be one of dereliction, he submitted that it may, have been in a poor condition but 
there was no evidence to suggest that it was incapable of being rendered suitable for 
occupation as a dwelling by the undertaking of a reasonable amount of repair work and it 
was not a truly derelict property.  
 
24. The panel noted the appellant’s argument that on the relevant date the property was not 
habitable, however, it was satisfied based on the evidence submitted that at the relevant date 
the physical state of the subject property could not be described as incapable of being 
repaired to make it suitable for its intended purpose. Furthermore, none of the problems 
identified, either individually or cumulatively, persuaded the panel that they were sufficient for 
the property to fail the hereditament test. The panel noted that photographs within the 
evidence appeared to demonstrate that the property was in poor condition and in need of 
repair, however, it found that at the relevant date the property was simply in disrepair and 
was capable of repair. It was not “truly derelict”, and no scheme of works was underway. 
 
25. The panel was therefore satisfied that at the relevant date the property would have been a 
hereditament under section 115 of the General Rate Act 1967 and that it did constitute a 
dwelling under section 3 of the Local Government Finance Act 1992. 
 

[2026] VTE VT00035003 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
6/6 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
26. Given that the panel had determined that the subject property was a dwelling, it had to be 
valued in line with the statutory assumptions that were contained within regulation 6 of the 
Council Tax (Situation and Valuation of Dwellings) Regulations 1992 (as amended); with one 
of the main assumptions being that the dwelling was in a reasonable state of repair, having 
regard to its age, locality and character. 
 
Conclusion 
 
27. In view of the above findings and conclusions, the appeal was dismissed. 
 
Right of further appeal 
 
28. Any party who is aggrieved at the Tribunal’s decision has a statutory right of further appeal to 
the High Court on a point of law pursuant to Regulation 43 of the Tribunal Procedure 
Regulations. A party does not require permission to appeal from the Tribunal. Any appeal 
must be made directly to the High Court using Form N161 (Appellant’s Notice) within four 
weeks of the date this decision and statement of reasons was issued. 
 
29. Further information regarding this statutory right of further appeal, and the parties’ other 
rights, is contained in the guidance booklet “A guide to tribunal decisions” available on the 
Tribunal’s website at www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk/guidance-booklets/.

DECISION 
 
1. 
The appeal is dismissed. 
 
2. 
The panel found nothing erroneous in the billing authority’s (BA) decision not to apply a 
discount for the period 28 July 2025 to 26 November 2025. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
The appeal was accepted by the Valuation Tribunal for England on 3 September 2025 as an 
appeal made under section 16 of the Local Government Finance Act 1992; that section 
allows challenges concerning council tax liability. 
 
4. 
The appeal challenges the billing authority’s decision of 11 November 2025 in respect of the 
empty property charge, which had been applied to the appeal property with from 28 July 
2025 to 26 November 2025 and the BA’s failure to grant exception under the Council Tax 
(Prescribed Classes of Dwellings) (England) Regulations 2003 (as amended); Class J, the 
property was vacant due to job-related circumstances. 
 
5. 
The appellant had contacted the clerk, Mrs Beresford, prior to the hearing to request that this 
matter be dealt with in his absence based on his written submission. 
 
6. 
This statement of reasons is not and does not purport to be a full verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Background 
 
7. 
On his appeal form the appellant stated as follows: 
 
“The authority has totally misunderstood the exemption/discount provision within SI 
2003/3011. This should provide for people in my circumstances the result that the liability for 
full council tax at 7 Westfield Rise (which I own) be discounted or waived in full.  
Their reasoning is flawed as I have no liability for Council Tax at The Vicarage as an office 
holder. The Diocese of Leeds has that liability and would only apply for a discount when that 
property was vacated on my retirement.”  
 
8. 
The BA argued that, in accordance with Regulation 6 of The Council Tax (Prescribed Classes 
of Dwellings) (England) Regulations 2003 (S.I. 2003/3011), the job-related council tax 
discount does not apply, on the grounds that, for the period from 28 July 2025 to 26 
November 2025, the property would be prescribed under Class C as an empty and 
unoccupied property. This council tax discount can only be awarded in cases where the 
property falls into either Class A or B, an empty but furnished property. 
 
Relevant Law 
 
9. 
The panel turned to SI 2003/3011 Council Tax (Prescribed Classes of Dwellings) (England) 
Regulations 2003 as amended: 
 
10. 4 Class A 

[2026] VTE VT00034809 (CTL) 
 
D1-BA Decision (v2603) 
3/5 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
The class of dwellings described in this regulation (“Class A”) comprises every chargeable 
dwelling in England— 
 
(a) which is not the sole or main residence of an individual; 
 
(b) which is furnished; and 
 
(c) the occupation of which is restricted by a planning condition preventing occupancy for a 
continuous period of at least 28 days in the relevant year; 
 
11. 5 Class B 
 
The class of dwellings described in this regulation (“Class B”) comprises every chargeable 
dwelling in England— 
 
(a) which is not the sole or main residence of an individual; 
 
(b) which is furnished; and 
 
(c) the occupation of which is not restricted by a planning condition preventing occupancy for 
a continuous period of at least 28 days in the relevant year; 
 
12. 7 Class C 
 
The class of dwellings described in this regulation (“Class C”) comprises every chargeable 
dwelling in England— 
 
(a) which is unoccupied; and 
 
(b) which is substantially unfurnished.  
 
13. SCHEDULE 
Job-Related Dwellings 
1 
 
(1) Subject to sub-paragraph (2), a dwelling is job-related for a person if it is provided for him 
by reason of his employment or for his spouse [or civil partner by reason of that person's] 
employment, in any of the following cases— 
 
(a) where it is necessary for the proper performance of the duties of the employment that the 
employee should reside in that dwelling; 
 
(b) where the dwelling is provided for the better performance of the duties of the employment, 
and it is one of the kinds of employment in the case of which it is customary for employers to 
provide dwellings to employees; 
 
(c) where, there being a special threat to the employee's security, special security 
arrangements are in force and the employee resides in the dwelling as part of those 
arrangements. 
 

[2026] VTE VT00034809 (CTL) 
 
D1-BA Decision (v2603) 
4/5 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
(2) If the dwelling is provided by a company and the employee is a director of that or an 
associated company, paragraph (a) or (b) of sub-paragraph (1) shall not apply unless 
either— 
 
(a) the employment is as a full-time working director, 
 
(b) the company is non-profit making, that is to say, it does not carry on a trade nor do its 
functions consist wholly or mainly in the holding of investments or other property, or 
 
(c) the company is established for charitable purposes only. 
 
14. 2A 
 
A dwelling is job-related for a person if he or his spouse or civil partner is a minister of any 
religious denomination and the dwelling is inhabited by him as a residence from which he 
performs the duties of his office. 
 
15. 14 Class J 
 
(1) The class of dwellings described in this regulation (“Class J”) comprises every chargeable 
dwelling in England— 
 
(a) where a qualifying person in relation to that dwelling is a qualifying person in relation to 
another dwelling in England, Wales or Scotland which for that person is job-related; or 
 
(b) which for a qualifying person is job-related where that person is a qualifying person in 
relation to another dwelling in England, Wales or Scotland. 
 
(2) For the purposes of— 
 
(a) paragraph (1)(a), a dwelling is job-related if it falls within the description set out in 
paragraph 1, 2 or 2A of the Schedule to these Regulations; 
 
(b) paragraph (1)(b), a dwelling is job-related if it falls within the description set out in 
paragraph 1 or 2 of that Schedule. 
 
16. 6 Exceptions 
 
Class A and Class B shall not include any dwelling which falls within the description of 
dwelling for Class J or Class K  
 
Discussion 
 
17. The panel noted that in the first instance on 29 July 2025 the appellant had stated that the 
property was furnished. On receipt of the council tax bill with a second home premium, he 
again contacted the BA on 20 August 2025 and stated that the property was unfurnished, a 
one-month 100% empty property discount was then applied. The appellant contacted the BA 
again on 30 September 2025 to question why the discount had only been applied for one 
month as he believed as a Vicar living in a job-related property he should be entitled to a 
discount for the full period.  
 

[2026] VTE VT00034809 (CTL) 
 
D1-BA Decision (v2603) 
5/5 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
18. The panel was aware that no further discount was available for a newly purchased property 
left vacant for job related purposes which had never been the sole or main resident of the 
owner. 
 
19. The panel noted that in his appeal documents the appellant had stated that the property 
became furnished with effect from 5 September 2025, and that he had advised the BA of this 
in a telephone conversation on 30 September 2025, but no record had been made of this in 
the BA’s submission. Have considered the documents submitted by the appellant, along with 
the chronology submitted by the BA the panel determined that insufficient evidence had been 
provided to support the appellant’s argument that the property was substantially furnished 
prior to him moving in. 
 
20. The appellant argued that the BA had misinterpreted the Council Tax (Prescribed Classes of 
Dwellings) (England) Regulations 2003, which had recently been amended. Having regard to 
that legislation the panel could find nothing erroneous in the BA’s interpretation. Exception J 
only applied to Classes A and B as cited above. 
 
Conclusion 
 
21. In view of the above findings and conclusions, the appeal was dismissed. 
 
Right of further appeal 
 
22. Any party who is aggrieved at the Tribunal’s decision has a statutory right of further appeal to 
the High Court on a point of law pursuant to Regulation 43 of the Tribunal Procedure 
Regulations. Any appeal must be made directly to the High Court using Form N161 
(Appellant's Notice) within four weeks of the date this decision and statement of reasons 
was issued. A party does not require permission from the Tribunal to appeal. 
 
23. Further information regarding this statutory right of further appeal, and the parties’ other 
rights, is contained in the guidance booklet “A guide to tribunal decisions” available on the 
Tribunal’s website at www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk/guidance-booklets/.

DECISION 
 
1. 
The appeal is allowed. 
 
2. 
The billing authority had not evidenced its local determination to charge a premium at 100% 
under section 11C of the Local Government Finance Act 1992. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
The appeal had been accepted by the Valuation Tribunal for England (VTE) as an appeal 
under section 16(1)(b) of the Local Government Finance Act 1992. This allows an aggrieved 
person to challenge the amount of council tax the billing authority has calculated that they 
are liable to pay. 
 
4. 
The dispute that the VTE had been asked to decide concerned the amount of the appellant’s 
council tax liability in respect of 2 Redwood Grove, Huddersfield HD5 9EQ, for the period 27 
June 2025 to 23 July 2025. In particular, the billing authority’s decision to charge a higher 
amount of 100% on top of the normal council tax, for dwellings which were unoccupied and 
substantially unfurnished. The appellant believes she should not be liable to pay a premium 
for the short period between purchasing the property and moving in. 
 
5. 
The billing authority’s representative had contacted the clerk, Mrs Beresford, prior to the 
hearing and requested that this matter be heard in her absence, based on the evidence pack 
provided. 
 
6. 
This statement of reasons is not and does not purport to be a full verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Background 
 
7. 
On her appeal form the appellant stated as follows: 
 
“On 28.06.2025 I bought a house at 2 Redwood Grove HD5 9EQ and move into this property 
within a month of purchasing it from 1 Glastonbury Drive Huddersfield HD3 4SA. Both 
properties are in band A, and I am entitled to a 25% discount as a single person.  The council 
wants £114.03 for empty and furnished premium and £27.01 transfers as at date of issue. In 
my opinion those charges are unfair and unreasonable  
I bought a new house and cannot moved there on the date of purchase as it is not 
possible.  Also, I do not know what they transfer as I have a different account number. It feels 
like a money grabbing attempt. I cannot afford it. The payment of £96 per month is excessive 
and is cause if destitution any additional charges will put me in debt! In addition, I asked for 
correction of the bill as I wish to pay monthly. I sent them emails on 18.10.2025, 22.11.2025 
and 03.12.2025 but never had any response. I do feel treated extremely unfairly by Kirklees 
Council and would like to ask you to help me”. 
 
8. 
The billing authority had accepted evidence from the appellant which showed the property to 
be unfurnished, and the empty and furnished premium had been removed, however, it had 
been replaced with a 100% empty and unfurnished premium so there was no difference to 
the amount of council tax charged. The 25% single person discount had been applied and 
backdated to the date the appellant had moved into the property.

Relevant Law 
 
9. 
The statutory framework for premium council taxes was provided by section 11B of the 1992 
Act (as amended).  This stated the following: 
 
11B Higher amount for long-term empty dwellings: England 
 
(1)   For any financial year, a billing authority in England may by 
determination provide in relation to its area, or such part of its area as it 
may specify in the determination, that if on any day a dwelling is a long-
term empty dwelling— 
 
(a) 
the discount under section 11(2)(a) shall not apply, and 
(b)   
the amount of council tax payable in respect of that dwelling and 
that day (“the relevant day”) shall be increased by such 
percentage of not more than the relevant maximum as it may so 
specify. 
 
(1A)  For the financial year beginning on 1 April 2019 the “relevant maximum” 
is 100. 
 
(1B)  For the financial year beginning on 1 April 2020 the “relevant maximum” 
is— 
 
(a)    in respect of any dwelling where the period mentioned in

100; 
(b)  
in respect of any dwelling where the period mentioned in 
subsection (8) ending on the relevant day is at least 5 years, 
200. 
 
(1C)  For financial years beginning on or after 1 April 2021 the “relevant 
maximum” is— 
 
(a)   
in respect of any dwelling where the period mentioned in 
subsection (8) ending on the relevant day is less than 5 years, 
100; 
(b)

subsection (8) ending on the relevant day is at least 5 years but 
less than 10 years, 200; 
(c)  
in respect of any dwelling where the period mentioned in 
subsection (8) ending on the relevant day is at least 10 years, 
300. 
 
(1D)  In exercising its functions under this section a billing authority must 
have regard to any guidance issued by the Secretary of State. 
 
(2)  The Secretary of State may by regulations prescribe one or more

(a)

dwellings;

the circumstances of, or other matters relating to, any person 
who is liable to the amount of council tax concerned. 
 
(4)  Where a determination under this section has effect in relation to a 
class of dwellings— 
 
(a)   
the billing authority may not make a determination under section 
11A(3), (4) or (4A) in relation to that class, and 
(b)  
any determination that has been made under section 11A(3), (4) 
or (4A) ceases to have effect in relation to that class. 
 
(5)  A billing authority may make a determination varying or revoking a 
determination under this section for a financial year, but only before the

and do so before the end of the period of 21 days beginning with the

ending with that day—

(9)  In determining whether a dwelling is a long-term empty dwelling, no

10. *** Prior to 1 April 2024, the period was two years rather than one year. 
 
Discussion 
 
11. In this appeal the panel had to be satisfied that respondent billing authority had correctly 
imposed a premium on the appellant at 100%. As no legislation set the 100% automatically, it

was necessary to be satisfied that a determination by full council had been made to adopt a 
premium of 100%. 
 
12. Section 11B (1) simply states: 
 
 11B Higher amount for long-term empty dwellings: England 
 
(1)   For any financial year, a billing authority in England may by determination 
provide in relation to its area, or such part of its area as it may specify in the 
determination, that if on any day a dwelling is a long-term empty dwelling— 
 
(a) 
  the discount under section 11(2)(a) shall not apply, and 
(b)   
the amount of council tax payable in respect of that dwelling and that 
day (“the relevant day”) shall be increased by such percentage of not 
more than the relevant maximum as it may so specify. 
 
13. The billing authority wanted the VTE to uphold its calculation to include a premium of 100%, 
which doubled the appellant’s council tax liability. The panel was aware that if an appeal 
challenges the billing authority’s decision to apply a premium under section 11B of the 1992 
Act, evidence is required to show that the billing authority has in fact made the relevant 
determination following its use of its devolved powers. If evidence is lacking within the 
submission to show that a determination has been properly made under section 11B of the 
1992 Act, the Tribunal may proceed on the basis that no determination has been made. It is 
insufficient for the billing authority to simply attest that a devolved determination has been 
made. Factual evidence must be provided to prove that the devolved powers have been 
properly exercised. 
 
14. The panel determined that in this appeal the billing authority’s evidential burden to show it 
had imposed an additional council tax amount on the appellant of 100% had not been 
discharged. In view of this, the panel decided that the appeal must therefore be allowed. 
 
Conclusion 
 
15. In view of the above findings and conclusions, the appeal was allowed. 
 
16. Accordingly, under the provisions of regulation 38(1) of the Valuation Tribunal for England 
(Council Tax and Rating Appeals) (Procedure) Regulations 2009, the Valuation Tribunal for 
England orders the billing authority to re-calculate the appellant’s council tax liability for the 
period 27 June 2025 to 23 July 2025 by removing the 100% premium. 
 
17. Under regulation 38(9), the billing authority must comply with this order within two weeks of

DECISION 
 
1. 
The appeal is allowed. 
 
2. 
The Tribunal decided to reduce the valuation band of the subject property from band E to 
band D with effect from 26 March 2025. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
The appeal process began when the appellant served a proposal on the respondent listing 
officer on 9 June 2025. In making the proposal, the appellant sought a reduction in the 
valuation list entry for the subject property from band E to band D. After considering the 
merits of the proposal, the listing officer determined that it was not well founded, issuing a 
decision notice to this effect on 25 September 2025. The appeal made to this Tribunal on 24 
November 2025 is against that decision. 
 
4. 
A joint evidence bundle had been provided by the listing officer, which had contributions from 
both parties to the appeal. It included photographs, the originating proposal, the listing 
officer’s decision, the appeal form submitted to the Tribunal, references to legislation, as well 
as evidence in respect of properties that the parties considered comparable to the subject 
property, to support their respective cases. 
 
5. 
To assist the lay appellant, with the agreement of the parties, the panel varied its model 
procedure and invited the listing officer’s representative to present her case first. 
 
6. 
This statement of reasons is not and does not purport to be a full verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Background 
 
7. 
The subject property was stated to be a detached house, built in the early 1990’s by Tarmac 
Homes. The appellant purchased the subject property on 26 March 2025 for £357,000. At the 
time of this purchase, according to the listing officer the property comprised three bedrooms, 
two living rooms, a kitchen, and two bath/shower rooms. It had a reduced covered area 
(RCA) of 99m2. The subject property was also stated to benefit from a conservatory and a 
single garage where one small vehicle could be parked.  
 
8. 
The property entered the valuation list at band E effective from 1 April 1993. Alterations to the 
subject property had been carried out by previous owners. The conservatory had been added 
to the subject property in 2011, albeit the parties could not confirm the precise date of this 
alteration. Although the conservatory addition did not affect the RCA size measurement of the 
property, the panel recognised that its addition was a ‘material increase’. With the appellant’s 
purchase, legally termed a ‘relevant transaction’, having taken place after this, the panel was 
satisfied that the appeal property had undergone a material increase, followed by a relevant 
transaction on 26 March 2025. As both limbs of the test had been satisfied the panel in 
reviewing the subject property’s band assessment was mindful that the relevant date at 
which they had to have regard to the physical state of the locality and the size, layout, and 
character of the dwelling was 26 March 2025.  
 

[2026] VTE VT00034017 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
3/8 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
9. 
The panel was required to determine the correct council tax band for the appeal property, 
based on the amount it might reasonably have achieved if sold by a willing vendor on the 
open market on 1 April 1991. The appellant sought a reduction to band D, but the listing 
officer maintained that band E was correct. 
 
Preliminary issues  
 
10. Prior to the hearing, the appellant had requested the respondent’s evidence be excluded as 
part of these proceedings, due to a delay in the listing officer’s evidence bundle being served 
on the appellant. This request was considered and declined by the Chair on 17 June 2026, 
with the parties informed that the appellant had not experienced any significant prejudice and 
that it would be disproportionate to exclude the respondent’s evidence. 
 
11. In advance of the hearing, the appellant drew attention to the fact that the joint evidence 
bundle did not include some pages of evidence submitted by him. The clerk to the hearing 
also found that information on certain pages within the combined evidence bundle did not 
show the full and complete information submitted by the appellant. The clerk to the hearing 
provided a copy of the missing and incomplete pages to the panel before the hearing date, 
with the parties also notified of this. The panel was satisfied that it was in receipt of all the 
evidence exchanged between the parties prior to the hearing date.  
 
12. The appellant referred to the inclusion of two pages within the evidence bundle that 
appeared to show the appeal he submitted to the Tribunal on 24 November 2025. The clerk 
clarified these were in fact pages automatically generated by the Tribunal’s computer system 
when the appellant’s appeal was received. The panel agreed to disregard these pages as 
part of the exchanged evidence.  
 
13. Prior to the hearing and also included within the appellant’s submission and evidence, the 
appellant stated vehemently that his appeal was in respect of the listing officer’s decision 
notice dated 25 September 2025. The clerk explained that the listing officer was not being 
obstructive in withholding details of the eight comparable properties referred to in the 
decision letter dated 25 September 2025, as legislation prevents specific property information 
from being included in such letters. The proper process is for the listing officer to identify the 
comparable properties it relies upon in its case submission six weeks before the hearing, 
after which the appellant may request sales evidence for a corresponding number of 
properties, provided they specify the addresses they wish to inspect. Although the properties 
were not identified in the decision letter, their addresses were supplied to the appellant by 
email on 20 May 2026, and, to the clerk's knowledge, no subsequent request for further 
details was made. The clerk also confirmed that the listing officer would rely only on the 
comparable properties listed in the notice issued under Regulation 17 Notice of The 
Valuation Tribunal for England (Council Tax and Rating Appeals) (Procedure) Regulations 
2009 and not on any other properties mentioned in the decision letter. The appellant could 
rely on comparable properties to which he had referred within his submission and evidence.  
 
Relevant Law 
 
14. Council tax had been introduced by the Local Government Finance Act 1992. This Act had 
been supplemented by a number of Statutory Instruments, in particular The Council Tax 
(Situation and Valuation of Dwellings) Regulations 1992, SI 1992/550 (as amended). 
 
15. The Council Tax (Situation and Valuation of Dwellings) Regulations 1992 requires that the 
value of a domestic property for council tax banding purposes was the amount which it might 

[2026] VTE VT00034017 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
4/8 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
reasonably have been expected to realise, as it physically existed at the relevant date, had it 
been sold on the open market by a willing vendor on the antecedent valuation date (AVD) of 
1 April 1991. Therefore, regardless of whether a property existed on 1 April 1991, or was 
purchased at a later date, in order to allow fairness and uniformity between all council tax 
valuations, all domestic property must be valued at the common date of 1 April 1991 and the 
level of value on that date, albeit within a range of values, had to be determined. 
 
16. The bands were set out in section 5(2) of the Local Government Finance Act 1992, with the 
relevant bands in this appeal being: 
• Band E - values greater than £88,000 but no more than £120,000 
• Band D - values greater than £68,000 but no more than £88,000 
 
17. In addition, Regulation 3 of The Council Tax (Alteration of Lists and Appeals) (England) 
Regulations 2009 (SI No 2009/2270), reads as follows: 
 
(3) No alteration shall be made of a valuation band shown in the list as applicable to the 
dwelling unless -  
 
(a) 
since the valuation band was first shown in the list as applicable to the dwelling –  
 
(i) 
there has been a material increase in the value of the dwelling and a relevant 
transaction has been subsequently carried out in relation to the whole or any 
part of it; or 
(ii) 
… ;  
 
18. Section 24(10) of the 1992 Act defined ‘material increase’ and ‘relevant transaction’ as: 
 
‘’material increase’ in relation to the value of a dwelling, means any increase which is caused 
(in whole or in part) by any building, engineering or other operation carried out in relation to 
the dwelling, whether or not constituting development for which planning permission is 
required.’ 
 
‘’relevant transaction’ means a transfer on sale of the fee simple, a grant of a lease for a term 
of seven years or more or a transfer on sale of such a lease.’ 
 
Discussion 
  
19. During oral evidence, both parties made reference to the relevant pages within the joint 
evidence bundle, to assist the panel. The appellant when presenting his case was reading 
from a twenty page ‘notes’ document that he had prepared in advance of the hearing. This 
had not been provided to the panel, the listing officer’s representative, or the clerk. Albeit the 
appellant was under no obligation to do so. Notwithstanding, there was a short adjournment 
during the appellant’s presentation.  
 
20. The appellant was advised by the panel that having read and reviewed the evidence bundle 
prior to the hearing it was preferable for the appellant to draw attention to the pertinent pages 
within the evidence bundle when making his arguments to support his case, rather than 
reading verbatim from the detailed twenty page document. It was not necessary for him to 
delve into the level of detail that the panel hitherto had heard from the appellant when 
reading from his ‘notes’. Moreover, the panel with the agreement of the listing officer’s 
representative, decided that the appellant would share his ‘notes’, after the conclusion of the 
hearing. The clerk received a hard paper copy of these notes from the appellant at the 

[2026] VTE VT00034017 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
5/8 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
hearing, with the appellant also emailing a copy post hearing to the clerk and the listing 
officer’s representative. The clerk forwarded these ‘notes’ to the panel. The panel gave 
regard to these notes, in relation to evidence exchanged between the parties prior to the 
hearing. Any information within the ‘notes’ about matters and evidence not exchanged 
between the parties prior to the hearing was disregarded.  
 
21. At the inception of council tax on 1 April 1993, the subject property was first entered into the 
valuation list at band E and remained at this band since then. In this appeal, the issue for the 
panel to determine, was the appropriate band based on the physical state of the locality and 
the size, layout, and character of the subject property on 26 March 2025, when it was 
purchased by the appellant. 
  
22. The panel considered, if available, that sales evidence in respect of the subject property and 
comparable properties that had completed at or around the AVD or the relevant date, would 
be pertinent and valuable evidence on which to determine the band. This evidence would be 
a useful indicator of value on the date that the property entered the valuation list at band E, 
or at the relevant date, to assist the panel in deciding the band based on open market 
values. The closer the comparability of a property to the subject property, and the nearer the 
date of the sale to the AVD or the relevant date, the more weight this evidence carried. Other 
evidence taken from the bands placed on comparable dwellings in the locality could also be 
considered as this can demonstrate a ‘tone’ of value of similar dwellings, which can be used 
to assist in establishing the correct council tax band. 
 
23. Turning first to the subject property, which had been sold on numerous occasions, the sale 
closest to the AVD was achieved at a value of £87,500, within the band D range of values, in 
December 1992, when there was no conservatory present. As aforementioned, the appellant 
purchased the property for £357,000 on 26 March 2025, with the conservatory, measuring 
8m2, in situ. The conservatory was not considered to be band significant.  
 
24. The panel noted the appellant’s remarks that the property did not comprise two separate 
living rooms. The respondent’s representative had inspected the property in May 2026, to 
verify the subject property’s RCA measurement, the inspection undertaken was external only. 
Nonetheless, during oral submissions the appellant stated that he had changed the internal 
configuration of the property after his purchase. The panel therefore had regard to the 
property as it existed on the relevant date when it comprised two living rooms.  
 
25. Both parties relied on comparable property evidence to support their respective positions. 
The listing officer placed primary weight on actual sales evidence close to the 1 April 1991 
AVD as well as the tone of bands established within the locality from properties of similar size 
and character.  
 
26. The respondent’s comparable property evidence consisted of eight properties, all with the 
same 99m2 RCA measurement as the subject property, comprising the same number of 
bedrooms, living rooms and bathrooms, and furthermore, all ascribed at band E. Three of 
these properties were on the same road as the subject property, Crane Close, four properties 
were on the neighbouring road of Curlew Close, with the remaining property situated on the 
neighbouring road of Heron Lane. The listing officer stated that all eight comparable 
properties were built by Tarmac Homes, underlining their comparability with the subject 
property. The panel was also informed that ten of the eleven houses on Crane Close were 
designated at band E, with one property at band D, this being 10 Crane Close, which was 
smaller with an RCA of 80m2.

D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
6/8 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
27. Turning to the listing officer’s sales evidence, the panel noted the properties with sales 
closest to the AVD were those at Curlew Close and Heron Lane. The sales achieved in 
September 1991, November 1991, and August 1992 respectively for numbers 3,1, and 7 
Curlew Close were all at the same value of £93,500. The house at 4 Curlew Close sold in 
April 1993 for £79,995, with 12 Heron Lane sold for £92,500 in August 1992. 
 
28. The sales of properties in Crane Close were more remote from the AVD, with 8 and 9 Crane 
Close sold in March and April 1993 for values of £76,995 and £79,995, respectively, with the 
sale of 2 Crane Close at a value of £87,500 in June 1995. 
 
29. The listing officer contended that during the late 1980s and early 1990s, the property market 
experienced a period of rapid growth, followed by a downturn, adding that property values 
did not return to their 1991 levels until the latter part of the 1990s and that accordingly, the 
sales evidence provided for the period 1991 to 1997 reflected market conditions prevailing at 
the time of each transaction. The respondent’s case submitted that the sales evidence 
demonstrates the fall in property values during the early to mid-1990s and shows how values 
subsequently recovered, returning to 1991 levels between 1995 and 1997 in the locality of 
the subject property, with the evidence indicating that the market began to decline in 1992 
and had started to recover by 1995, with values returning to 1991 levels between 1995 and 
1997. 
 
30. The appellant contended that the listing officer is incorrect in stating that the property market 
declined after 1991 and cites the sales of 2, 3 and 4 Crane Close as examples. The sale of 2 
Crane Close in June 1995 for £87,500 was preceded by a sale in January 1993 for £79,995. 
Both properties at 3 and 4 Crane Close sold in December 1992 for £74,995 and achieved 
respective sales in May 1996 of £84,000 and in December 1995 of £83,000. The respondent 
asserted however, that these earlier sales took place between 1992 and 1993, during a 
period when the housing market was in decline. 
  
31. Referring the panel to the properties at Crane Close and Curlew Close mentioned above, the 
appellant argued that the detached dwellings at Curlew Close benefited from wider 
frontages, larger driveways, larger plot sizes, and superior side access compared with the 
subject property. The appellant further contended that these properties were located on a 
more attractive street and were predominantly corner-plot houses, whereas the subject 
property was situated mid-street. In the appellant’s view, these factors contributed to the 
Curlew Close properties having a higher market value than the subject property. In support of 
this contention, he stated that the differences between the three sales of 1, 3, and 7 Curlew 
Close between September 1991 and August 1992 at £93,500 in comparison to the sales of 3 
and 4 Crane Close in December 1992 for £74,995, further highlighted this point. 
 
32. The respondent referred to the sale of 12 Heron Lane, which it stated had one sided access 
similar to the subject property, yet sold for £92,500 in August 1992, well within the band E 
range of values. It sold later in May 1995 for £89,950 showing that the housing market in the 
locality was falling. The appellant asserted that this property is situated in a far better and 
more attractive road with grassed areas and large trees in extra land between the pavement 
and the street in front of some houses and some very well kept gardens. with the sheer size 
of the very much larger plots opposite 12  Heron Lane evident from the location map 
included within the evidence bundle. In addition, Heron Lane was stated as having the 
convenience of abundant street parking of which Crane Close has none. According to the 
appellant, the property at 12  Heron Lane is not directly comparable to the subject property. 
Moreover, he stated that when 12 Heron Lane was for sale it was considered for purchase in 
March 2025 however the asking price was out of the appellant’s reach, with its sale for 

[2026] VTE VT00034017 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
7/8 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
£398,000 in April 2025, a month after the relevant date, signifying it was more valuable than 
the subject property. 
 
33. During verbal questioning the appellant stated to the panel that he considered the best 
comparable property to be 5 Pheasant Close. Whilst ascribed at band E, this was a four 
bedroom detached house, referred to in the listing officer’s decision notice, which he 
provided information about to support his contention that this was larger than the subject 
property, with a bigger garage and also built by Bryant Homes, who were regarded to have 
built better quality houses in the locality than those built by Tarmac Homes. It sold less than 
three weeks after the AVD, in April 1991 for £90,000. With this sale circa £2,000 above the 
band D range of values more or less at AVD, for a larger and better property than the subject 
property, this was a strong indication that the subject property at the AVD would have sold in 
the band D range of values. 
 
34. The panel considered this finely balanced appeal. Although the respondent relied on 
evidence suggesting a decline in the housing market following the 1 April 1991 antecedent 
valuation date, the panel found that the sales evidence presented a mixed picture, with some 
transactions indicating a falling market while others suggested values remained stable or 
recovered within a relatively short period.  
 
35. Significant weight was attached to the subject property's own sale in December 1992 for 
£87,500, which fell within the band D range and constituted the most direct evidence of its 
value, together with several other comparable sales that also fell within or close to the upper 
end of the band D range. The panel also noted the appellant’s evidence regarding 5 
Pheasant Close, a larger four-bedroom Bryant Homes property that sold for £90,000 in April 
1991, only marginally above the band D threshold, which it considered a strong indicator that 
the appeal dwelling would likewise have fallen within band D. The panel further accepted that 
a number of the respondent’s principal comparables, particularly those at Curlew Close and 
12 Heron Lane, possessed slightly enhanced characteristics when compared with the subject 
property, including larger plots, wider frontages, superior access arrangements and, in some 
instances, a more favourable setting. Although the panel acknowledged that many similar 
properties in the locality were assessed in band E and considered the respondent’s evidence 
relating to market fluctuations during the early 1990s, having regard to the totality of the 
evidence, the panel concluded on the balance of probability that the subject property’s value 
at the relevant date would be greater than £68,000 but no more than £88,000. 
 
Conclusion 
 
36. In view of the above findings and conclusions, the panel in this appeal deemed that the 
available evidence and oral submissions demonstrated that band E was excessive for the 
subject property, with band D appropriate, effective from 26 March 2025. The appeal was 
allowed. 
 
Order  
 
37. Accordingly, we order under the provisions of regulation 38(2) and (9) of the Valuation for 
Tribunal England (Council Tax and Rating Appeals) (Procedure) Regulations 2009, the listing 
officer to alter the valuation list within two weeks of the date of this order to show the 
valuation list entry in respect of 7 Crane Close, Stratford-upon-Avon, CV37 9EE at band D 
with effect from 26 March 2025.

DECISION 
 
 
1. 
The appeal was dismissed.  
 
2. 
The panel confirmed band E with effect from 31 October 2024 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
The appellant served a proposal on the Listing Officer (LO) on 19 June 2025 to challenge the 
council tax band. In making the proposal they sought a band C entry. After considering the 
merits of the proposal, the LO determined that it was not well founded and a Decision Notice 
to this effect was issued on 23 December 2025.   
 
4. 
The appellants appealed to this Tribunal against the decision notice on 9 January 2026.   
 
5. 
This statement of reasons is not and does not purport to be a full verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Background  
 
6. 
The appeal property was a detached house that had been newly built by Linden Homes on 
the Spark Mill Meadows Development which was situated 31 miles from York and 8 miles 
from the centre of Hull. The house type was known as ‘The Pembroke’. It had a reduced 
covered area (RCA) of 147m2.  
 
7. 
The accommodation on the ground floor consisted of a living room, open plan kitchen / dining 
/ family area, utility, study and W/C. On the first floor there was a master bedroom complete 
with en-suite, a further three bedrooms and a family bathroom. It also benefited from a single 
garage. It was purchased by the appellants for £359,950 on 31 October 2024.   
 
Relevant Law 
 
8. 
Regulations 6(1) and 6(2) of the Council Tax (Situation and Valuation of Dwellings) 
Regulations 1992 (as amended) provide that the value of a dwelling shall be taken to be the 
amount which it would, subject to certain assumptions, reasonably have been expected to 
realise if sold on the open market by a willing vendor on the antecedent valuation date (AVD) 
of 1 April 1991, irrespective of whether it actually existed on this date. 
 
9. 
The bands under consideration in this appeal and the respective ranges of values, as at the 
AVD level of values, were as follows:  
 
Band C – values exceeding £52,000 but not exceeding £68,000; 
Band D - values exceeding £68,000 but not exceeding £88,000; 
Band E – values exceeding £88,000 but not exceeding £120,000.   
 
10. The panel was therefore required to determine the band applicable to the appeal dwelling on 
the basis of its sale in a hypothetical transaction at the AVD. 
 

[2026] VTE VT00034772 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
3/4 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
11. In deciding this appeal, the panel must weigh all the evidence presented but the best 
evidence must always be sales at or close to the AVD; either on the subject property or ones 
similar to it, as stated in the High Court decision of Domblides v Listing Officer [2008] EWHC 
3271 (Admin), referred to in the respondent’s case. This judgment provides guidance on the 
weight to be attached to different types of evidence in such valuation appeals.  
 
12. The physical state of the property and its locality are taken to be as they were at the “relevant 
date” which, for the purposes of this appeal, was 31 October 2024, this being the date on 
which the property entered the valuation list at Band E.  
 
Discussion 
 
13. The appellant felt it was unfair that the LO had placed the appeal property in band E when 
they were informed by the council and building developer that it would be in band C. The 
appellants stated that they had carefully budgeted their finances and would not be able to 
sustain living at the property as the council tax bills were too high. The appellants explained 
that they were disappointed in the system and felt that the LO and council should be more 
integrated to provide a fairer system. They also felt that the council tax band was too high 
considering the road was not fully adopted by the council and that they were paying a private 
maintenance charge.  
 
14. In support of band E, the LO provided the details of eight comparable properties, four of 
which had sold close to the AVD. These properties ranged in size from 116m2 to 139m2 and 
were all in band E. The closest sale to the AVD was 53 Central Avenue which was situated 
0.82 miles from the appeal property. This property was smaller at only 116m2 and it had one 
less bedroom. It had sold for £95,000 on 15 March 1991. The band had been established 
since 1 April 1993 and had not been challenged.  
 
15. The LO provided three four-bedroom properties which were 2 Sackville Close, 125m2 in size 
and had sold for £91,000 on 25 January 1991. The council tax band E had been confirmed 
by the Tribunal in 1999. 42 St Matthews Court measured 139m2 and had sold for £90,000 on 
18 September 1991. This property had been in the council tax list since 1 April 1993 and had 
no challenges. 45 Chester Avenue measured 130m2 and had sold for £98,950 on 17 
February 1993. This property had also been in the council tax list since the commencement 
of the list, over thirty years ago with no challenges.  
 
16. The LO had also provided four properties to reference that there was an established tone for 
similar sized properties in the locality. These properties measured between 112m2 and 
139m2. Three of the properties have been heard by the Tribunal and had the bands 
confirmed at band E in 1995, 1998 and more recently in 2026. The other property had been 
in the council tax list since 2016 and had not been challenged.  
 
17. Having regard to the evidence presented, the panel were not persuaded that band E was 
incorrect for the appeal property. The strong sales evidence presented by the LO showed 
that smaller properties that had sold close to the AVD did achieve values in excess of 
£88,000.  
 
18. At the hearing the appellants did refer to two comparable properties, one of which it was 
thought to be a composite, meaning part domestic and part non-domestic. Usually, properties 
of this type have a lower council tax band due to certain ties that are associated with the 
property. However, it was noted by the panel that the two properties referred to by the 
appellants were not contained within the evidence pack and no details had been provided 

[2026] VTE VT00034772 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
4/4 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
other than addresses. Although the LO did not raise any objections to these two properties, 
the panel placed little weight on them as firstly, there was a lack of detail to ascertain whether 
they could be comparable to the appeal property or not, certainly the composite property was 
not considered like for like. Secondly, these were provided as tonal evidence as no sales had 
been provided for them, and the LO’s sales evidence presented was stronger.  
 
19. The panel noted the appellant’s concern regarding the provisional band which had been 
placed upon the appeal dwelling by the local billing authority. This was simply an 
administrative mechanism which was intended to provide the appellant with the ability to 
make payments in respect of their council tax liability for the appeal property prior to the band 
being determined by the LO. The provisional band had no bearing upon the actual band that 
entered the valuation list which was the sole responsibility of the LO. 
 
20. The panel also considered the appellant’s submissions regarding the fact the appeal property 
was located on an unadopted road and their obligation to pay an annual service charge. 
However, the panel was not presented with sufficient evidence to show that this would have 
any detrimental impact on value at the AVD and, if it did, that it was band significant.   
 
21. Therefore, based on the evidence presented, the panel confirmed band E for the appeal 
property.

DECISION 
 
1. 
The appeal is dismissed. 
 
2. 
The panel determined that the conditions for Class G exception from the premium for long 
term empty dwellings were not met. The subject property had been marketed for sale for one 
year from 8 June 2023 and therefore, the premium had been correctly applied from 20 March 
2025. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
The appeal challenges the Respondent Billing Authority’s decision of 2 September 2025 in 
respect of the premium for long term empty dwellings, which has been applied to the subject 
property with effect from 20 March 2025.  
 
4. 
The Appellant disagreed with the decision, arguing that the subject property was being 
actively marketed for sale and should therefore be exempt from the premium under Class G. 
The basis for her appeal on 20 September 2025, was that the period that the subject 
property was marketed for sale prior to 1 November 2024 should not be considered by the 
Respondent, as government guidance was not published until that date. 
 
5. 
This statement of reasons is not and does not purport to be a full verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Background 
 
6. 
The subject property became empty and unfurnished following the vacation of the tenant on 
20 March 2023. As the owner of the property, the Appellant was made liable from that date.  
 
7. 
From 8 June 2023, the Appellant entered into a contract with Richard James Estate Agents 
to sell the subject property on the open market. 
 
8. 
After the subject property had been empty and unfurnished for two years, the Respondent 
applied a premium of 100% to the chargeable amount for council tax from 20 March 2025.  
 
9. 
On 12 March 2025, the Appellant provided the Respondent with evidence to demonstrate 
that the subject property had been actively marketed for sale from 8 June 2023 and, 
consequently, the premium should not be applied. The subject property subsequently sold on 
28 August 2025.  
 
10. In reviewing the evidence provided, the Respondent determined that the Class G exception 
from the higher amount for long term empty dwellings was not applicable on the basis that 
the subject property had been marketed for sale for over twelve months prior to 1 April 2025 
and therefore, the subject property did not meet the requirements set out in legislation. 
 
Relevant Law 
 
11. Part I of the 1992 Act makes provision for billing authorities in England and Wales to levy a 
tax, known as council tax, in respect of domestic hereditaments (“dwellings”) in their 
administrative areas.

12. Section 11(2) of the Act makes provision for a discount in the amount of council tax payable 
in prescribed conditions, including where there is no resident of the dwelling.  So far as is 
relevant, it provides:

section 11B of the Act relating to the imposition of premiums.

15. The Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023 (“the 2023 Act”) changed the definition of a 
long-term empty dwelling from a property that had been unoccupied and substantially 
furnished for two years to one year, provided that the requirements for Section 11B had been 
met. In this case, the Respondent Billing Authority decided not to amend the definition of a 
long-term empty dwelling under its own local scheme. On 21 February 2021, the Respondent 
made a determination for a premium of 100% to be applied to the chargeable amount for 
council tax on any property that had been unoccupied and unfurnished for two years. 
 
16. The regulations referred to in Section 11D(1) are the Council Tax (Prescribed Classes of

inserted. These Regulations prescribe the classes of dwelling in relation to which a billing 
authority may not make a determination to apply a higher amount of council tax (referred to 
as ‘exceptions’). Relevant to this appeal:

G for a further period unless the dwelling has been the subject of a 
relevant transaction. 
 
(3) 
For the purposes of this regulation— 
 
(a) 
marketing a dwelling for sale means the marketing for sale 
of— 
 
(1) the freehold; or 
(2) a leasehold for a term of seven years or more; 
 
(b) 
“excepted period” is a period during which a dwelling falls 
within Class G. 
 
Discussion 
 
17. The issue for the panel to decide in this case was whether the Respondent Billing Authority 
was correct not to award the Class G exception for the period between 20 March 2025 and 
28 August 2025. There had been no disagreement between the parties that the Appellant 
was the owner of the subject property. Additionally, both parties accepted that the subject 
property was empty and unfurnished from 20 March 2023. The dispute, therefore, concerned 
whether the Respondent’s interpretation of the amendments to the legislation that took effect 
the financial year beginning on 1 April 2025 was correct. 
 
18. When considering the case, the panel focused on whether the subject property met the 
criteria for properties actively marketed for sale as set out in legislation. If it was determined 
that the requirements for the criteria had been met, then the exception for dwellings marketed 
for sale could be applied to the chargeable amount for the subject property. In coming to a 
decision on the appeal, the panel considered that the criteria relevant to this case were: 
 
(a) 
that is being marketed for sale at a price that is reasonable for the sale 
of the dwelling,  
… 
unless it has been such a dwelling for a period of one year or more. 
 
19. In analysing the evidence before it, the panel identified that an email from Richard James 
Estate Agents had been provided by the Appellant to the Respondent, along with the link to 
the advertisement for the property on RightMove. In the email dated 20 March 2025, the 
panel confirmed that the property had been marketed for sale on the open market from 8 
June 2023. Per the advertisement on RightMove, the property had initially been marketed for 
sale at £270,000 and had been reduced to £240,000. Additionally, in her bundle, the 
Appellant advised the panel that she had accepted an offer for the property for £238,000 on 
23 April 2025, with a completion date of 28 August 2025. Accordingly, the panel was satisfied
