D1-BA Decision (v2603) 
7/9 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
that the subject property had been actively marketed for sale for the period between 8 June 
2023 and 28 August 2025. 
 
20. The panel noted the Appellant’s argument that Government guidance on the exceptions 
classes had not been published until 1 November 2024. As such, the Appellant argued this 
was the first date that the subject property should be considered as having been marketed 
for sale. However, the panel considered this interpretation to be incorrect.  The panel had 
regard to regulation 3 of the Council Tax (Prescribed Classes of Dwellings) (England) 
Regulations 2003, which provides that the Class G exception to the council tax premium 
could only take effect from 1 April 2025. Accordingly, the panel found that, although 
Government guidance was published on 1 November 2024, the prescribed Class G 
exception itself did not come into force until 1 April 2025. Therefore, the only period that the 
exception could apply, provided the requirements were met, would from 1 April 2025 until the 
property was sold. 
 
21. In presenting her case to the panel, the Appellant argued that the above Government 
guidance was not issued until 1 November 2024. Therefore, any period that the property was 
marketed for sale prior to that date should not be considered, when applying the exception to 
the chargeable amount for council tax. The Appellant submitted that the purpose of the 
guidance was to avoid penalising owners who were actively seeking to bring properties back 
into use and argued that it was unfair for the exception period to be exhausted before the 
start of the financial year in which the premium became payable. In addition, the Appellant 
advised the panel that she had been informed on four separate occasions by the 
Respondent that the premium would not apply to the chargeable amount of council tax for 
the subject property. The Appellant argued that she had relied upon this advice and had a 
reasonable expectation that the premium would not be imposed. 
 
22. In response to the appeal and presentations to the panel, the Respondent’s representative 
disputed the Appellant’s interpretation of the legislation. It took a literal interpretation of the 
wording of the legislation and argued to the panel that it was clear and deliberate. The billing 
authority’s stance was that the exception could only be considered for one year and did not 
exclude the period prior to the legislation coming into force. In her presentation to the panel, 
the Respondent’s representative advised that the Appellant had been encouraged to apply 
for a Section 13A (1) (c) discretionary discount under its local scheme but, as of the hearing, 
no application had been received. Accordingly, the Respondent’s representative argued that 
it was correct in determining that the Class G exception could not be applied at any point 
during the period in dispute. 
 
23. Having considered the submissions of both parties, the panel determined that the availability 
of the Class G exception from 1 April 2025 did not automatically entitle a property to relief if it 
had currently been on the market for sale. To qualify, the property had to satisfy the statutory 
criteria for the exception. The panel found that the subject property had been actively 
marketed for sale for more than twelve months before 1 April 2025 and therefore did not 
qualify for any period of exemption under Class G. While the panel accepted that the 
Respondent Billing Authority had previously advised the Appellant that the premium would be 
removed, the panel found that the Respondent had erred in its previous claims and, as such, 
were entitled to correct the chargeable amount for council tax for the Appellant in line with 
legislation. As the property had been unoccupied since 20 March 2023, the premium under 
section 11B became payable on 20 March 2025, two years after the property became 
unoccupied and unfurnished.

8/9 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
24. The Appellant submitted that the Respondent had not provided prior notification that the 
premium for long-term empty dwellings would be applied to her council tax account. Under 
questioning, the Respondent’s representative confirmed that notice of the premium had not 
been published in a local newspaper following the determination made on 21 February 2021, 
as required by section 11B(6) of the Act. However, the representative stated that details of 
the determination had been made available on the Council’s website. In considering this 
issue, the panel found that, under section 11B(7) of the Act, a failure to comply with 
subsection (6) does not affect the validity of the determination. Accordingly, the panel 
concluded that the Respondent’s failure to publish the notice in a local newspaper did not 
invalidate the decision to impose the premium. The panel therefore found that the premium 
had been lawfully applied and that the absence of newspaper publication did not provide 
grounds for allowing the appeal. 
 
25. The panel accepted that the Appellant found it unfair for the period of sale to be considered 
prior to 1 April 2025, however, perceived unfairness arising from the policy choice to apply a 
premium of 100% for council tax on long-term empty dwellings was a matter for Parliament, 
not for this Tribunal. The panel’s role in this case was limited to applying the law as enacted. 
 
26. Accordingly, the panel found that the Respondent could only apply an exception from 1 April 
2025, but the length of the exception was governed by when the property was first marketed, 
not by when the revised legislation would take effect. 
 
Conclusion 
 
27. In view of the above findings and conclusions, the panel was satisfied that the Class G 
exception could not be applied prior to 1 April 2025 and the requirements for the Class G 
exception were not met after 1 April 2025. 
 
28. Accordingly, the appeal was dismissed. 
 
Right of further appeal 
 
29. Any party who is aggrieved at the Tribunal’s decision has a statutory right of further appeal to 
the High Court on a point of law pursuant to Regulation 43 of the Tribunal Procedure 
Regulations. Any appeal must be made directly to the High Court using Form N161 
(Appellant's Notice) within four weeks of the date this decision and statement of reasons 
was issued. A party does not require permission from the Tribunal to appeal. 
 
30. Further information regarding this statutory right of further appeal, and the parties’ other 
rights, is contained in the guidance booklet “A guide to tribunal decisions” available on the

DECISION 
 
1. 
The appeal is dismissed. 
 
2. 
The Tribunal finds that the subject property comprised one hereditament but two self-
contained units, both of which had correctly attracted a separate entry in the valuation list. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
This appeal relates to a proposal to merge the two council tax entries at 15A and 17 
Shepherds Lane (the subject property). 
 
4. 
On 15 May 2025, the Appellant served a proposal on the Respondent Listing Officer. In his 
proposal, the Appellant requested a merger of the two entries in the valuation list with effect 
from 27 February 2025. 
 
5. 
On 3 December 2025, after considering the merits of the proposal, the Respondent Listing 
Officer determined that the proposal was not well founded and a decision notice to that effect 
was issued. 
 
6. 
On 30 January 2026, the Appellant filed an appeal with this Tribunal. 
 
7. 
This statement of reasons is not and does not purport to be a full verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Background 
 
8. 
The subject property was constructed in 1881 as a single dwelling. In the 1980s, the property 
was converted into two separate flats. 15A Shepherds Lane, the first floor flat, was entered 
into the valuation list at band B from 1 April 1993. Prior to merging the property, 15A 
Shepherds Lane comprised of three bedrooms, one bathroom, one reception room and one 
kitchen. 17 Shepherds Lane, the ground floor flat, was entered into the valuation list at band 
D from 1 April 1993. Prior to merging the property, 17 Shepherds Lane comprised of two 
bedrooms, one bathroom, one reception room and one kitchen. Following the decision to 
utilise the subject property as one dwelling, the subject property was comprised of three 
bedrooms, two bathrooms, four reception rooms, one kitchen, and one utility room. 
 
9. 
The Appellant initially purchased 15A Shepherds Lane in 1982 with a leasehold interest in 
the property. Subsequently, 17 Shepherds Lane was purchased by the Appellant in 
November 2023, along with the freehold for the entirety of the property.  
 
10. Following the completion of the sale, the Appellant commenced works to merge the two 
separate flats into one dwelling. As part of the works, the Appellant converted the kitchen on 
the first floor into a utility/laundry room and removed the timber infill wall in the entryway for 
15A Shepherds Lane, allowing access to all floors of the property through one entry point. 
 
11. The Listing Officer determined that no change would be made to the valuation list, deeming 
the existing two entries in the list correct on the basis that both 15A Shepherds Lane and 17 
Shepherds Lane remained self-contained units within one hereditament. 
 

[2026] VTE VT00035328 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
3/8 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
Relevant Law 
 
12. Part I of the Local Government Finance Act 1992 (the Act) makes provision for billing 
authorities in England and Wales to levy a tax, known as council tax, in respect of domestic 
hereditaments (“dwellings”) within their area.   
 
13. Section 3 of the Act provides— 
 
3 Meaning of “dwelling” 
 
… 
 
(2) 
Subject to the following provisions of this section, a dwelling is any 
property which— 
 
(a) 
by virtue of the definition of hereditament in section 115(1) of the 
General Rate Act 1967, would have been a hereditament for the 
purposes of that Act if that Act remained in force; and  
 
(b) 
is not for the time being shown or required to be shown in a local 
or a central non-domestic rating list in force at that time; and  
 
(c) 
is not for the time being exempt from local non-domestic rating for 
the purposes of Part III of the Local Government Finance Act 
1988. 
 
14. The definition of dwelling essentially referred back to the definition of a ‘hereditament’ under 
section 115(1) of the General Rate Act 1967, which stated the following:  
 
115 Interpretation  
 
(1) 
In this Act, except where the context otherwise requires, the following 
expressions have the following meanings respectively, that is to say— 
 
… 
 
" hereditament " means property which is or may become liable to 
a rate, being a unit of such property which is, or would fall to be, 
shown as a separate item in the valuation list; 
 
15. The issue of self-contained units was covered in section 3(5) of the 1992 Act and the Council 
Tax (Chargeable Dwellings) Order 1992 (SI No 1992/549), as amended. Articles 2 and 3 of 
the Order specified that:  
 
“2.  ‘single property’ means property which would, apart from this 
Order, be one dwelling within the meaning of section 3 of the 
Act; and “self-contained unit” means a building or part of a 
building which has been constructed or adapted for use as 
separate living accommodation. 
 
3.  
Subject to article 3A where a single property contains more than one 
self-contained unit, for the purposes of Part 1 of the Act, the property

4/8 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
shall be treated as comprising as many dwellings as there are such 
units included in it and each such unit shall be treated as a dwelling.”  
 
 
16. The Appellant, in his bundle, also referred to Article 4 of the 1992 Order, which states:  
 
4 
 
(1) 
Where, subject to article 3C, a multiple property— 
 
(a) 
consists of a single self-contained unit, or such a unit 
together with or containing premises constructed or adapted 
for non-domestic purposes; and 
 
(b) 
is occupied as more than one unit of separate living 
accommodation, 
 
the listing officer, may, if he thinks fit, subject to paragraph (2) below, treat the 
property as one dwelling. 
 
(2) 
In exercising his discretion in paragraph (1) above, the listing officer 
shall have regard to all the circumstances of the case, including the 
extent, if any, to which the parts of the property separately occupied 
have been structurally altered. 
 
17. Relevant to this appeal, Article 2 of the 1992 Order defines a “multiple property” as: 
 
““multiple property” means property which would, apart from this 
Order, be two or more dwellings within the meaning of section 3 of 
the Act” 
 
18. Prior to the hearing, the clerk circulated to the panel and the parties’ copies of the following 
judgments Corkish v Wright and Hart [2014] EWHC 237 (Admin) and Daniels (LO) v Aristides 
[2006] EWHC 3052 (Admin), which was circulated to the panel and the parties by the clerk 
prior to the hearing. 
 
19. The following case law was also referred to by the Respondent, in the evidence and during 
the hearing: 
 
Salisbury v Bunyan [2021] EWHC 3136 (Admin) 
Coleman (LO) v Rotsztein [2003] EWHC 1057 (Admin) 
Batty v Burfoot and Others [1995] RA 299 
McColl v Subacchi (LO) [2001] EWHC 712 (Admin) 
Jorgensen (LO) v Gomperts [2006] EWHC 1885 (Admin)   
Ramdhun v Valuation Tribunal of England [2014] EWHC 946 (Admin) 
 
Appeal to the Tribunal 
 
20. This appeal was made under regulation 10 of the Council Tax (Alteration of Lists and 
Appeals) (England) Regulations 2009 (SI 2009 No 2270). Relevant to this appeal it provides: 
 
10 Disagreement as to proposed alteration

(1) 
Where the LO has— 
 
(a) 
made a decision under regulation 9(1)(b)(iv); and 
 
(b) 
served a decision notice on the proposer in accordance 
with regulation 9(2), 
 
the proposer or any competent person may appeal to the VTE against the 
LO's decision. 
 
… 
 
Discussion 
 
21. Firstly, it was not contended by either party that there was more than one hereditament; both 
15A and 17 Shepherds Lane were in the same rateable occupation. Ms Murray sought to 
defend the entries in the valuation list on the basis that there was one hereditament that 
comprised two self-contained units. The panel was therefore satisfied that it could proceed 
on the basis there was only a single hereditament and that the question to be answered was 
whether that hereditament contained two self-contained units of living accommodation. 
 
22. Having regard to the relevant statutory provisions, the panel considered that the Listing 
Officer was required to treat part of a dwelling as a separate “self-contained unit” where it 
had been adapted for, or was capable of, use as separate living accommodation. The issue 
for determination was therefore whether the subject property was capable of use as two 
separate units of living accommodation. 
 
23. The Listing Officer explained that a self-contained unit would ordinarily include independent 
access, either by way of its own entrance or through a communal area, together with facilities 
for living and sleeping, washing facilities including a toilet, and basic facilities for the 
preparation of food. 
 
24. The panel turned to the High Court judgment of Corkish (LO) v Wright and Hart. In this case, 
Popplewell J derived six principles from former authorities, which have been set out below: 
 
(1) 
The question is whether the effect of the construction or adaptation is 
such as to make the relevant building or part of a building reasonably 
suitable for use as separate living accommodation. I prefer the 
expression “reasonably suitable” for such use to “capable” of such use, 
because it makes clear that what matters is its fitness for that purpose 
by reference to contemporary standards of what is reasonable, not 
merely whether it might conceivably be used for such purpose however 
remote the possibility.  
 
(2) 
The question is to be answered by reference to the physical 
characteristics of the building. This is sometimes referred to as a “bricks 
and mortar test”, but the epithet does not accurately capture the wide 
range of physical characteristics which may be of relevance including 
services and fixtures.  
 

[2026] VTE VT00035328 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
6/8 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
(3) 
This is an objective test. The test is not concerned with when, how or 
why those characteristics were achieved. The purpose of the 
construction or adaptation is irrelevant. The test is addressed to the 
result of the building work, not the circumstances in which it was carried 
out. Intention is irrelevant.  
 
(4) 
Whether the test is met is a matter of fact and degree for the tribunal.  
 
(5) 
There is a divergence in the authorities as to whether the actual use to 
which the building has been or is being put is capable of being a 
relevant consideration. The decision attaches to the dwelling through 
changes of ownership and use, such that actual use at any given time 
will rarely help to inform the result of applying an objective test based 
on the physical characteristics of the building. I prefer the view that 
actual use may in some cases be of some relevance. If, for example, 
the part of the property has in fact been used, or is being used, for 
occupation by persons who do not form part of a single household with 
those who occupy the remainder of the property, that may be a factor 
which supports a conclusion that its physical characteristics make it 
suitable for such occupation. However actual use is not the test, and 
even in cases where it may be of some relevance it will not usually be a 
factor of significant weight. At most it may reinforce a decision reached 
by reference to the physical characteristics of the building.  
 
(6) 
If what is being considered is part of a building, the physical 
characteristics to be considered include those of the remainder of the 
building as well as the part being considered. Access is one aspect of 
such characteristics. Separate public access may be a pointer to the 
part being separate living accommodation; whereas if access is through 
the remainder of the building this may tell against the part being 
separate living accommodation. In the latter case different weight may 
be attached where access is through the living areas of the remainder 
of the building from the weight to be attached where it is through a 
hallway. But access is not a factor which can be determinative without 
considering the other physical aspects of the building. The weight to be 
attached to it is a matter for the tribunal. 
 
25. Thus, in deciding this appeal, the panel must consider whether the physical characteristics of 
the subject property made it reasonably suitable for use for two separate living units of 
accommodation. 
 
26. With the above considerations in mind, the panel turned to the arguments and evidence 
presented on behalf of the Respondent Listing Officer. It was the view of Ms Murray that 
there had not been any significant alterations to the subject property in order for it to be 
merged into one assessment. In particular, Ms Murray argued that, while the cooker had 
been removed from the former kitchen on the first floor, facilities for basic food preparation 
remained in place, such as countertops and a sink, indicating that 15A Shepherds Lane 
remained a self-contained unit and, therefore its entry could not be merged for the purposes 
of council tax.   
 
27. After considering the representations from the Respondent, the panel then turned to the 
arguments and evidence submitted by the Appellant. The Appellant argued that the intention 

[2026] VTE VT00035328 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
7/8 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
upon purchasing the second flat, 17 Shepherds Lane, was to convert the subject property 
back into a single dwelling as it was now being utilised as one residential unit. The Appellant 
advised the panel that the water accounts for both properties had been combined and that 
the entire property now operated under a single postal address. To facilitate the merger of the 
two properties, the Appellant advised that the cooker and associated wiring had been 
removed from the first-floor kitchen, which was now used as a utility/laundry room.  
 
28. While the panel accepted that the Appellant’s intention and use of the hereditament was as 
one dwelling rather than two self-contained units, it found that, per Corkish v Wright and Hart, 
these factors were not considered as part of the test. The panel had to consider the physical 
characteristics of both 15A and 17 Shepherds Lane at the proposed effective date. On the 
evidence, the panel considered that the subject property was capable of being used as two 
self-contained units, as both parts contained all the essential elements of a habitable space. 
The panel found that there was no internal photographic evidence of the subject property 
provided by either party, and the sole evidence available to it was a proposed plan of 
changes and planning documents from Dartford Council, neither of which were substantial 
enough to demonstrate that the two flats were no longer self-contained. 
 
29. The panel reached this conclusion notwithstanding the absence of an oven. It noted that the 
first-floor flat retained facilities for basic food preparation, including a sink, work surface, and 
an electricity supply capable of supporting domestic appliances. The panel therefore 
considered that the absence of an oven did not materially affect the flat’s suitability for use as 
living accommodation. In Daniels (LO) v Aristides, Davis J had commented that the presence 
of an oven was not a decisive factor at paragraph [27] of the judgment: 
 
27.  The question of whether or not cooking facilities are or are not crucial in 
a context such as the present was discussed in the case of Jorgensen 
v Gomperts … It seems to me that the judge in that case was correct in 
saying it all depends on the particular circumstances of the particular 
case: sometimes it will be of decisive importance perhaps, and 
sometimes it will not be of decisive importance at all.” 
 
30. In addition, the Appellant stated that the timber infill wall separating the entrance hall of 15A 
Shepherds Lane from the adjoining property had been removed. The Appellant advised that 
the removal of this wall created a single point of access serving both parts of the property 
and provided internal access throughout. The Appellant argued that, as a result, the 
properties no longer had separate means of access and could not readily be occupied as 
separate independent living accommodation. 
 
31. The panel had regard to McColl v Subacchi, in which it was held that access arrangements to 
a self-contained unit, whilst a relevant consideration, is not itself determinative. The fact that 
access may be obtained through the main dwelling does not, of itself, deprive 
accommodation of its character as a self-contained unit. Sir Christopher Bellamy at 
paragraph [27] of that judgment commented: 
 
27. …the question of separate access, while a highly material factor, is not 
an essential condition of "separateness" for the purposes of the 
construction of the Order. 
 
32. In view of the case law and the evidence before it, the panel found that access was not an 
issue in this case as 15A Shepherds Lane did not require access through the living area of 

[2026] VTE VT00035328 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
8/8 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
17 Shepherds Lane. To access the unit on the first floor, the panel found that it could be 
accessed through a communal hallway, rather than through a private area that would impact 
the physical enjoyment of the unit. 
 
33. In addition to the physical changes made to the subject property, the Appellant argued that 
the Listing Officer had failed to exercise her discretion under Article 4 of the Council Tax 
(Chargeable Dwellings) Order 1992 to treat the subject property as a single dwelling. The 
panel noted that Article 4 relates to ‘multiple property’ as detailed in paragraph 17 of this 
decision and was not relevant to the case before it.  
 
34. Having regard to the physical characteristics of the subject property as a whole, the panel 
noted that it was possible to access both units via communal areas. The panel also 
determined that someone could quite comfortably reside at either property, as they each had 
all the necessary living facilities for basic food preparation, sleeping, living and bathing; both 
the flats were reasonably suitable for use as separate living accommodation. The panel 
accepted that the cooker had been removed from the kitchen area in the first floor flat and 
the installation points had been removed. However, the panel remained of the opinion that 
the flat provided all the hallmarks of a self-contained unit.  
 
Conclusion 
 
35. In view of the above findings and conclusions, the panel was satisfied that the subject 
property had been correctly assessed as a single hereditament which contained two self-
contained units that were both capable of use as separate living accommodation. 
 
36. Accordingly, the appeal was dismissed.   
 
Right of further appeal 
 
37. Any party who is aggrieved at the Tribunal’s decision has a statutory right of further appeal to 
the High Court on a point of law pursuant to Regulation 43 of the Tribunal Procedure 
Regulations. A party does not require permission to appeal from the Tribunal. Any appeal 
must be made directly to the High Court using Form N161 (Appellant’s Notice) within four 
weeks of the date this decision and statement of reasons was issued. 
 
38. Further information regarding this statutory right of further appeal, and the parties’ other 
rights, is contained in the guidance booklet “A guide to tribunal decisions” available on the 
Tribunal’s website at www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk/guidance-booklets/.

DECISION

2.

2025 and therefore its entry should remain in the valuation list. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
This appeal relates to a proposal to delete the subject property’s entry from the council tax 
valuation list. 
 
4. 
On 3 July 2025, the Appellant served a proposal on the Respondent Listing Officer. In her 
proposal, the Appellant requested the deletion of the assessment of the subject property from 
the valuation list with effect from 20 May 2025. 
 
5. 
On 14 October 2025, after considering the merits of the proposal, the Respondent Listing 
Officer determined that the proposal was not well founded and a decision notice to that effect 
was issued. 
 
6. 
On 13 January 2026, the Appellant filed an appeal with this Tribunal. 
 
7. 
This statement of reasons is not and does not purport to be a full verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Background 
 
8. 
The subject property was an end terrace house that entered into the valuation list at band D 
from 19 June 2017 as a new property. It measured 110m2 reduced covered area (RCA) and 
comprised of two bedrooms and two bathrooms.  
 
9. 
In her appeal to the Tribunal, the Appellant contended that the subject property was 
uninhabitable due to serious health and safety risks caused by a brown water leak and a 
subsequent ant infestation. The Appellant advised that, as a result of the safety concerns and 
remedial works, she had to vacate the subject property with her child as she could not safely 
occupy the property. The Appellant confirmed that the works to repair the subject property 
had been conducted between 20 May 2025 and 1 February 2026. 
 
10. Mr Short contended that the subject property remained a hereditament. For a property to no 
longer be a hereditament for the purposes of council tax, it would have to be incapable of 
being repaired to make it suitable for its intended purpose. In this case, he contended that 
the repair works were remedial, rather than structural, in nature. As such, Mr Short argued 
that the repairs were not unreasonable or too extensive to complete. 
 
Relevant Law 
 
11. Part I of the Local Government Finance Act 1992 (the “Act”) makes provision for council tax 
to be payable in respect of domestic hereditaments (“dwellings”) within their administrative 
areas. The term ‘dwelling’ is defined in section 3 of the Act as follows:  
 

[2026] VTE VT00034863 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
3/7 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
3 Meaning of “dwelling” 
 
… 
 
(2) 
Subject to the following provisions of this section, a dwelling is any 
property which— 
 
(a) 
by virtue of the definition of hereditament in section 115(1) of the 
General Rate Act 1967, would have been a hereditament for the 
purposes of that Act if that Act remained in force; and  
 
(b) 
is not for the time being shown or required to be shown in a local 
or a central non-domestic rating list in force at that time; and  
 
(c) 
is not for the time being exempt from local non-domestic rating for 
the purposes of Part III of the Local Government Finance Act 
1988. 
 
12. The definition of dwelling essentially refers back to the definition of a ‘hereditament’ under 
section 115(1) of the General Rate Act 1967, which stated the following:  
 
115 Interpretation  
 
(1) 
In this Act, except where the context otherwise requires, the following 
expressions have the following meanings respectively, that is to say— 
 
… 
 
" hereditament " means property which is or may become liable to 
a rate, being a unit of such property which is, or would fall to be, 
shown as a separate item in the valuation list; 
 
13. If it is determined that a dwelling exists, then the Council Tax (Situation and Valuation of 
Dwellings) Regulations 1992 (SI 1992 No. 550) (the “Valuation Regulations”) requires the 
Listing Officer to make a number of assumptions when valuing a dwelling for entry in the list. 
Relevant to the subject appeal Regulation 6(2)(e) of the Valuation Regulations requires that 
the Listing Officer, and now on appeal, the Tribunal, assumes “that the dwelling was in a 
state of reasonable repair.”  
 
14. The panel must therefore determine whether, considering the physical state of the subject 
property, it remained a dwelling. If it did, the statutory valuation assumptions were engaged.  
 
15. The Respondent Listing Officer relied on and gave reference to the following case law:  
 
• 
Newbigin v Monk [2017] UKSC 14  
• 
Wilson v Coll [2011] EWHC 2824 (Admin)  
• 
Jackson (VO) v Canary Wharf Limited [2019] UKUT 136 (LC) 
• 
Bunyan v Patel [2022] EWHC 1143 (Admin)  
 
Appeal to the Tribunal 
 

[2026] VTE VT00034863 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
4/7 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
16. This appeal was made under regulation 10 of the Council Tax (Alteration of Lists and 
Appeals) (England) Regulations 2009 (SI 2009 No 2270). Relevant to this appeal it provides: 
 
10 Disagreement as to proposed alteration 
 
(1) 
Where the LO has— 
 
(a) 
made a decision under regulation 9(1)(b)(iv); and 
 
(b) 
served a decision notice on the proposer in accordance 
with regulation 9(2), 
 
the proposer or any competent person may appeal to the VTE against the 
LO's decision. 
 
… 
 
Discussion 
 
17. When considering the facts of the case, the panel accepted that repair work was required at 
the subject property to bring it back into use. For council tax purposes, that alone was not 
sufficient for the entry of the subject property to be deleted from the valuation list. For its 
entry to be deleted, the panel must be satisfied that it did not constitute a dwelling. If the 
panel concluded that the dwelling continued to exist, then it must be valued on the statutory 
assumption that it was in reasonable repair, even if in reality it was in need of repair. 
 
18. In determining whether a dwelling exists, the High Court’s judgment in Wilson is relevant. At 
paragraphs 40 and 41, Singh J stated:  
 
“40.  … I accept that as a general matter of law the crucial distinction for the 
purposes of deciding whether there is, or continues to be, a 
hereditament should focus upon whether a property is capable of being 
rendered suitable for occupation (in the present context occupation as a 
dwelling) by undertaking a reasonable amount of repair works. The 
distinction …, in my view, is between a truly derelict property, which is 
incapable of being repaired to make it suitable for its intended purpose, 
and repair which would render it capable again of being occupied for 
the purposes for which it is intended. 
 
“41.  The crucial distinction in that regard is not between repairs which would 
be economic to undertake or uneconomic to undertake.”  
 
19. In Patel, Lang J affirmed the test expounded in Wilson as the correct one to be applied when 
determining whether a hereditament was still in existence (see paragraph [48] of that 
judgment).  
 
20. Thus, in determining whether a hereditament exists, one must consider “having regard to the 
character of the property and a reasonable amount of repair works being undertaken could 
the premises be occupied as a dwelling?” 
 
21. In her proposal to the Respondent Listing Officer, the Appellant detailed the works required to 
bring the property back into use due to the water ingress and the subsequent ant infestation. 

[2026] VTE VT00034863 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
5/7 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
The Appellant advised that the property required the removal and replacement of the floors 
and the kitchen to allow for an investigation into the cause of the leak to be carried out. 
Additionally, she advised that she had to vacate the subject property with her young child due 
to health and safety concerns caused by the brown water leak. 
 
22. With the above considerations in mind, the panel turned to the arguments and evidence 
presented on behalf of the Respondent Listing Officer. It was Mr Short’s opinion that the 
subject property was not derelict, with the required repair works being remedial in nature, 
rather than structural. Mr Short argued that no evidence had been provided to suggest that 
the subject property was not a dwelling as at the proposed effective date, or from any other 
date, and it had therefore not ceased to be a dwelling for council tax purposes. 
 
23. After considering the submissions made on behalf of the Respondent Listing Officer, the 
panel turned to the evidence and arguments presented by the Appellant. In the bundle, the 
Appellant provided fifteen photographs taken between May 2025 and January 2026 of the 
work carried out at the subject property. Upon reviewing the photographs, the panel found 
that the majority of the works conducted were carried out on the ground floor of the subject 
property and the ensuite bathroom but did not impact the property in its entirety. Additionally, 
based on the photographs, the panel noted that there was evidence that the subject property 
did not have what could be considered as a functional kitchen while investigative works were 
carried out, however, the connection points remained in place to allow for installation. 
Therefore, the panel determined that the evidence provided was not sufficient to demonstrate 
that the subject property could not be utilised as a dwelling with reasonable repair. 
 
24. In addition to the photographs, the panel was provided with a copy of a Quality Surveyor’s 
report completed by PBA Planning following a visit to the subject property on 3 June 2025. 
The panel found that the report concluded that the soil pipe serving the main bathroom had 
been leaking since the subject property was first occupied and that the extensive ant 
infestation at the property had been caused by the leak. One of the recommendations arising 
from the report was that the Appellant should vacate the subject property. However, upon 
reviewing the document, the panel found that the inspection was focused solely on the 
kitchen area, rather than the subject property as a whole. Consequently, the panel found the 
report was limited in scope and did not provide a comprehensive assessment of the overall 
condition or habitability of the property. While the report identified defects and recommended 
temporary vacation of the property, the panel noted that it did not conclude that the dwelling 
was incapable of repair within its character or that there were structural concerns as a result 
of the brown water leak.  
 
25. The final piece of evidence provided to the panel by the Appellant was an ant control report 
prepared by PGH Pest Prevention in 2025. The panel found that the report identified nine ant 
nests within the kitchen area and a further nest in the ensuite bathroom. The panel noted that 
the report also suggested that the infestation was likely linked to a long-standing leak from 
the soil pipe, which had created conditions conducive to ant activity. Whilst the panel 
acknowledged that the infestation and associated damage required extensive investigative, 
remedial and pest control works, it found that the report was primarily concerned with 
identifying the source of the infestation and recommending measures to eradicate it. The 
panel determined that the recommended works were directed towards the investigation, 
treatment and repair of defects that were capable of being remedied, and the report did not 
conclude that the subject property was beyond repair, structurally unsound, or truly derelict.  
 
26. In reviewing the evidence, the panel turned to the principles established in Newbigin v Monk 
and Jackson v Canary Wharf. Although these cases concerned non-domestic rating, the 

[2026] VTE VT00034863 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
6/7 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
panel considered them relevant in assisting with the determination of whether a hereditament 
continued to exist. The case law established that a property could cease to be a 
hereditament where it was undergoing a scheme of reconstruction or redevelopment that 
rendered it incapable of beneficial occupation whilst in a transitional state. However, having 
considered the Appellant’s evidence and the nature of the works undertaken, the panel found 
that the subject property had been undergoing remedial repair and reinstatement works 
arising from a leaking soil pipe and ant infestation, rather than a programme of 
reconstruction, redevelopment, or structural alteration. The works were intended to restore 
the property to its previous condition and did not alter its use, layout, character, or identity as 
a dwelling. Furthermore, during the hearing, the panel found that the duration of the works 
had been significantly influenced by the investigation and processing of the home warranty 
claim, rather than by the scale or complexity of the physical works themselves. Therefore, the 
principles of Newbigin v Monk and Jackson v Canary Wharf did not apply to this case. 
 
27. Having regard to the above conclusions, the panel found that the subject property could not 
be regarded as a truly derelict property that was incapable of occupation for its intended use 
with a reasonable amount of repair; this was supported by the fact that the property had been 
repaired by the time that the appeal had been initiated. The subject property was therefore a 
hereditament (a dwelling) and the statutory assumption of reasonable state of repair had to 
be applied in the valuation. 
 
Conclusion 
 
28. In view of the above findings and conclusions, the panel was satisfied that the subject 
property remained a dwelling. Therefore, its entry should remain in the valuation list. 
 
29. Accordingly, the appeal was dismissed.  
 
Right of further appeal 
 
30. Any party who is aggrieved at the Tribunal’s decision has a statutory right of further appeal to 
the High Court on a point of law pursuant to Regulation 43 of the Tribunal Procedure 
Regulations. A party does not require permission to appeal from the Tribunal. Any appeal 
must be made directly to the High Court using Form N161 (Appellant’s Notice) within four

DECISION

2. 
The panel found that the appeal property should not be deleted from the council tax valuation 
list on 3 December 2020. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
This appeal had been brought in respect of the following: the appellant was the owner and 
council taxpayer of the property 10 Dorset House, Portland Road, Bishops Stortford, 
Hertfordshire CM23 3RU. 
 
4. 
The appellant had submitted a proposal on 4 December 2024 to delete the property from the 
council tax valuation list with effect from 3 December 2020 as it was uninhabitable due to a 
fire. 
 
5. 
The listing officer (LO) issued her decision notice on 3 November 2025 maintaining the 
property in the council tax list. 
 
6. 
The appellant appealed to the tribunal on 9 January 2026.  
 
7. 
To assist the appellant and with the agreement of the parties, the tribunal panel varied its 
model procedure and invited the LO’s representative to present his case first. 
 
8. 
This tribunal decision document is not and does not purport to be a verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Relevant Law 
 
9. 
The appeal property could only be deleted from the valuation list if it had ceased to be a 
‘dwelling’. The term ‘dwelling’ is defined within Section 3(2) of the Local Government Finance 
Act 1992 as: 
 
“...any property which -  
 
(a) by virtue of the definition of hereditament in Section 115(1) of the General Rate Act 
1967, would have been a hereditament for the purposes of that Act if that Act 
remained in force; and 
(b) is not for the time being shown or required to be shown in a local or a central non-
domestic rating list in force at that time; and 
(c) is not for the time being exempt from local non-domestic rating for the purposes of 
Part III of the Local Government Finance Act 1988”    
 
10. The term ‘hereditament’ is taken from Section 115(1) of the (now repealed) General Rate Act 
1967 as: 
 
“…property which is or may become liable to a rate, being a unit of such property 
which is or would fall to be, shown as a separate item in the valuation list.” 
 

[2026] VTE VT00034302 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
3/4 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
11. A ‘dwelling’ is a unit of property which must appear as a separate entry in the valuation list if 
it is not required to appear in a non-domestic rating list or is not exempt from non-domestic 
rating. Once it has been established that a dwelling exists, it must be valued in accordance 
with the statutory assumptions contained within the Council Tax (Situation and Valuation of 
Dwellings) Regulations 1992 and, in particular, regulation 6(2)(e) “that the dwelling was in a 
reasonable state of repair”, even if the reality is very different.  
 
12. Council Tax (Alteration of Lists and Appeals) (England) Regulations 2009.  
 
13. Council Tax (Situation and Valuation of Dwellings) Regulations 1992.  
 
14. Relevant Case Law: 
 
Wilson v Coll (LO) [2011] EWHC 2824 (Admin) 
Bunyan v Patel [2022] EWHC 1143 (Admin) 
SJ & J Monk (A Firm) v Newbigin (Valuation Officer) [2017] UKSC 14 
Jackson (VO) v Canary wharf Limited [2019] UKUT 136 (LC)  
 
Issue 
15. The issue for the panel to determine was whether the appeal property should be deleted 
from the council tax list with effect from 3 December 2020 for a period of 12 months.  
 
Discussion 
 
16. The respondent had provided a consolidated evidence bundle totalling containing the 
information which had been exchanged between the parties prior to the hearing. This 
included a copy of the proposal, the appeal, the decision notice, photographs of the appeal 
property and extracts from the relevant legislation and case law. The date on which to 
consider the appeal property, the proposed effective date, was 3 December 2020.  
 
17. The appellant stated that a fire had occurred at around 10 or 11pm on Thursday 3 December 
2020 in the upstairs bedroom whilst the property was let out to tenants. The fire took hold in 
the bedroom and spread into the hall but did not go beyond, there was extensive smoke 
damage in every room in the flat and in the loft space. The Fire Service was called and put 
out the fire. 
 
18. The accommodation of the appeal property consisted of one bedroom, a bathroom, hall and 
open-plan kitchen / diner / lounge and all the surfaces and fixtures were either charred or 
smoke damaged. In the communal stairwell all the walls and ceiling were smoke affected and 
required redecoration. He had also included a copy of the Insurance payout which was 
mainly was for the loss of rent.  
 
19. In his opinion, the appeal property could not be legally occupied as it was uninhabitable for 
12 months from 3 December 2020.  
  
20. The LO’s representative stated that the property had suffered a fire and there was some 
smoke damage, however, the structure of the property remained intact and the property 
merely required repair. It was wind and watertight, there was no scheme of works being 
undertaken and the property was not truly derelict. For these reasons, the appeal property 
should remain in the list. 
 

[2026] VTE VT00034302 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
4/4 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
21. The panel noted the comments of the appellant is respect of the appeal property not being 
habitable as the damage was more than just repairs, it was extensive. However, whether a 
property is habitable or not is not the required test.  
 
22. The panel was aware that for a property to be removed from the council tax list it would need 
to have reached the state of being truly derelict, for example, if the roof or external walls were 
missing or where normal repairs would not bring it into a condition that would make it fit for 
occupation.  
 
23. The panel referred to the case of Wilson v Coll where the judge outlined the stages to follow 
when considering a dwelling in poor repair. The panel must consider if a dwelling exists. If it 
does, then the panel must assume reasonable repair. When considering whether a 
hereditament exists, the panel asked "Having regard to the character of the property and a 
reasonable amount of repair works being undertaken could the premises be occupied as a 
dwelling?".  
 
24. The panel noted that the fire report stated that the fire was confined mainly to the bedroom of 
the flat but there was no damage to any structural elements of the property. The insurance 
report referred to stripping out, cleaning, redecoration and replacement of fixtures, all of 
which the panel found constituted reasonable repair, they were not substantial and were not 
throughout all aspects of the appeal property.   
 
Decision  
 
25. The panel found that the appeal property therefore remained to be a hereditament and 
therefore a dwelling for the purposes of council tax on 3 December 2020. 
 
26. The panel therefore dismissed the appeal.

15. The appellant’s representative had stated that the property was last used on 15 January 
2025 and the WC facilities were removed on 16 January 2025. The billing authority (BA), 
Haringey Council, had undertaken a review of lettable properties in its area and found that 
the appeal property was too small to be rented out as a flat. The BA required a minimum of 
13m2 in area and the flat was only 9m2. The licence to let the flat was revoked on 20 June 
2025 and the room was now used as a utility room. 
 
16. For these reasons the appellant wanted the property deleted from the council tax list. 
 
17. The respondent’s representative had stated that the appeal property remained intact, was 
wind and watertight, was not derelict, there was no scheme of works being undertaken and it 
was in reasonable repair. There was no reason to delete the appeal property as it remained 
to be a dwelling for the purposes of council tax.  
 
18. The panel noted that the appeal property had been in the council tax valuation list since 25 
June 2012 as a council tax dwelling and had been let out until January 2025. The panel was 
aware that the size of the dwelling was not a part of its consideration, that had only been 
relevant to the BA’s own procedures, it had no bearing on the appeal property as a council

minimum space standards, licensing restrictions, or the legal permissibility of occupation 
under housing legislation was not relevant.

for council tax purposes since 25 January 2012 and remained to be a hereditament and a 
dwelling for council tax purposes on 16 January 2025.

21. The panel found that the appeal property must remain in the council tax valuation list and the 
appeal was therefore dismissed.

STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
This appeal had been brought in respect of the following: the appellant was the owner of the 
properties 8 and Flat Bst 8A Leinster Gardens, London W2 6DP. The 16 flats comprising 8 
Leinster Gardens were merged by the listing officer (LO) to form one property in band H on 1

separately in the council tax list in band B with effect from 17 July 2020.  
 
4. 
The appellant had submitted a proposal on 17 April 2025 to merge the basement flat with 8 
Leinster Gardens to form one property. 
 
5. 
The LO issued her decision notice on 9 December 2025 declining to merge the assessments. 
 
6. 
The appellant appealed to the tribunal on 9 January 2026.  
 
7.

8.

On 24 November 2008 it was split into 18 separately assessed flats, Flats 1 to 18, each in

9. 
On 23 August 2009, Flat 17 was deleted with effect from 1 February 2009 as “no longer in

10. On 5 August 2013, Flats 16 and 18 were deleted from the list with effect from 3 November

11. On 7 February 2021, Flat Bst 8A Leinster Gardens was brought into the list in band B with

12. On 20 March 2024, following the introduction of new legislation, The Council Tax

Issue 
13. The issue for the panel to determine was whether Flat Bst 8A Leinster Gardens should be 
merged with 8 Leinster Gardens with effect from 1 December 2023.

Discussion 
 
17. The panel was aware that prior to the Chargeable Dwellings amendment separately occupied 
/ tenanted rooms in a property were separately assessed for council tax as they were 
separate hereditaments for the purposes of Section 3(2) of the LGFA 1992 and Section 
115(1) of the General Rate Act 1967 and therefore separately banded. These kinds of 
properties did not have to be self-contained units.  
 
18. Further, article 4 of the Chargeable Dwellings Order allowed the LO discretion to treat a 
multiply occupied property, a house in multiple occupation (HMO), as a single dwelling 
depending on its structure and adaptation. 
 
19. From 1 December 2023 when the Chargeable Dwellings Amendment became law the LO 
had to aggregate a property consisting of separate hereditaments into one single band where 
the properties met the legal requirements.  
 
20. The panel understood that the LO had merged the flats at 8 Leinster Gardens in accordance 
with the amendment and therefore had to consider whether the basement flat should also be 
merged. 
 
21. The appellant’s representative stated that, in his opinion, there was only one property on the 
site 8 Leinster Gardens and it consisted of 19 flats in total, three self-contained flats in the 
basement and sixteen flats from the ground floor up.  
 
22. He explained that, in 2020, the billing authority had received an application for benefits in 
respect of one of the flats in the basement and advised the LO who subsequently created a 
separate entry in the council tax list, 8A Leinster Gardens, even though there were in fact 
three flats there.

254 Meaning of “house in multiple occupation” 
 
(1) For the purposes of this Act a building or a part of a building is a “house in multiple 
occupation” if— 
 
(a) it meets the conditions in subsection (2) (“the standard test”); 
(b) it meets the conditions in subsection (3) (“the self-contained flat test”); 
(c) it meets the conditions in subsection (4) (“the converted building test”); 
(d) an HMO declaration is in force in respect of it under section 255; or 
(e) it is a converted block of flats to which section 257 applies. 
 
(2) A building or a part of a building meets the standard test if— 
(a) it consists of one or more units of living accommodation not consisting of a self-contained 
flat or flats; 
(b) the living accommodation is occupied by persons who do not form a single household 
(see section 258); 
(c) the living accommodation is occupied by those persons as their only or main residence or 
they are to be treated as so occupying it (see section 259); 
(d) their occupation of the living accommodation constitutes the only use of that 
accommodation; 
(e) rents are payable or other consideration is to be provided in respect of at least one of 
those persons' occupation of the living accommodation; and 
(f) two or more of the households who occupy the living accommodation share one or more 
basic amenities or the living accommodation is lacking in one or more basic amenities. 
 
25. He contended that 8 Leinster Gardens met the conditions of (1) (a), “the standard test”, there 
were no self-contained units of accommodation and the entire property should therefore be 
considered as one HMO.  
 
26. He confirmed that there had always been three flats in the basement, at least since 2007. He 
had also included a copy of the BA’s HMO Licence dated 28 July 2022. The panel noted that 
it was valid from 24 November 2021 to 23 November 2026 for a maximum of 38 people living 
as 19 households. The licence listed the lettable properties and the appellant’s 
representative stated that Bedrooms 1, 2 and 3, Lower Ground Floor, Front, Middle / Rear 
and Rear respectively were the three basement flats.  
 
27. The LO’s representative stated that the merger of the 15 flats had been done in accordance 
with the amendment legislation, however, the basement was not included. This was because 
the basement was separate to the rest of the building and had two separate external access 
points.  
 
28. The panel noted that the basement flats were contained within the HMO licence for 8 
Leinster Gardens but found that this was not determinative as to whether they were self-
contained or not. It appeared to the panel that the BA had notified the LO of one of the 
basement flats simply in order to make an assessment for benefits purposes, however, it had 
issued a licence that included three basement flats but had not reported the other two flats to 
the LO for assessment.  
 
29. The panel noted that there was no disagreement between the parties that the flats from the 
ground floor upwards should be classed as one HMO. The HMO licence stated that there 
was a bathroom located on mid floor level, 1st and 2nd and on the fourth floor, middle, and

30. The panel noted that the appellants’ representative had stated that the three flats in the 
basement were self-contained, that the facilities in the upper floors were not shared with the 
basement flats. Further, that the basement flats were not connected internally to the upper 
floors, there was clear separation, which the panel found to be a crucial factor, and they had 
their own two separate external access points.  
 
31. The panel found that the basement flats were separate self-contained units of 
accommodation and were therefore not part of the HMO at 8 Leinster Gardens as they did 
not meet the requirements of the Council Tax legislation.  
 
32. The appellant’s representative had queried that there must be many other properties in the 
same situation, however, the panel were only concerned with the matter under appeal before 
it. 
 
Decision  
 
33. The panel found that Flat Bst 8A Leinster Gardens was not part of the HMO at 8 Leinster 
Gardens and must remain as a separate entry in the council tax valuation list. 
 
34. The panel therefore dismissed the appeal.
